meta.title: Budget Tracker specification
meta.product: A personal / household budget tracker. A budget starts from the monthly total of its incomes, is split into categories and subcategories with a monthly expectation each, and is tracked period by period against the transactions the user records. It also tracks subscriptions, debts, and the planned flow of money between accounts. CHF only. UI in English and French.

glossary.definition: The container of everything else: incomes, categories, subscriptions, debts, transactions, periods and accounts. Always a monthly budget.
The member who created the budget. Only the owner can delete it, change its end date, or manage members and invitations.
A person who belongs to a budget (the owner included). Every member can read and edit everything in the budget.
An offer to join a budget, addressed by the owner to an email address. The invited person accepts or declines it after signing in with a matching verified email.
A monthly amount with a nominal pay day, belonging to one member of the budget. The incomes of a budget sum into its monthly total.
The one income of a budget whose pay dates define the periods.
The day of the month an income is due, for example the 25th, before clamping to the month length and before the weekend rule.
The date an income is really paid in a given month: the nominal pay day clamped to the month length, then moved by the weekend rule (or overridden by hand).
Per income: how a pay day that falls on a Saturday or Sunday moves. One of nearest (default), previous, next, none.
The span from one actual pay date of the primary income to the day before the next one. A stored row with a start and an end date.
The period that contains today. The last period that exists as a row; its end date is a projection.
The point between the end of one period and the start of the next. It can be moved by hand; a manual boundary is never recomputed.
The current period end computed as the day before the next actual pay date of the primary income.
The 1-based number of a period within its budget. Income validity and versions refer to it, not to dates.
An income is in force in a period when it started at or before that period and has not ended before it; a version is in force when it is the latest one effective at or before that period.
Of a period: the sum of the incomes in force in that period, each at the version in force for that period.
The sum of all incomes of the budget; the amount the budget starts from.
The terms of an income (and later of a category expectation, a subscription or a debt) in force from a given period on. Edits create versions; they never rewrite the past.
The first level of the budget split, for example insurance. Holds the monthly expectation when it has no subcategories.
The optional second (and last) level under a category, for example insurance/car.
The amount planned for a category or subcategory per month, entered per month or per year.
Of a period: its income total minus the sum of the expectations in force in that period. Negative when more is assigned than the income.
What is left of a category within a period. Reset at the end of each period.
The surplus or deficit of a period: its income total minus the total spent in it. Per category: the expectation minus what was spent.
An amount on a date, in a category or subcategory, with an optional description and an optional link to a debt or a subscription.
A recurring charge with a price, a first charge date, a cadence (monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or yearly) and a category.
When a subscription will next be charged.
Money owed, with a principal, an optional interest rate and a planned monthly payment.
What is still owed on a debt; transactions assigned to the debt reduce it.
A place money is kept (salary account, savings, third pillar, tax reserve), possibly at different banks.

A planned movement of money between two accounts, scheduled as an offset in days from an income's actual pay date (such as "payday + 2 days: 1000 CHF from A to Savings") or on a fixed day of the month. Flagged automatic or manual.
A planned transfer done by a standing order; assumed done.
A planned transfer the user makes by hand; shown as a per-period checklist.
The plan of transfers between accounts after payday, drawn as a diagram.
Bulk creation of transactions through the one import function in the database, from a paste/CSV screen, a repository script a Claude session can run, and later a connector.
The mark an imported transaction carries until the user has checked it.
A saved mapping from a merchant to a category, so categorisation of imports improves over time.
The hundredth of a Swiss franc (centime). Every amount is an integer number of rappen.
Swiss franc, the only currency.
The calendar date in Europe/Zurich, decided by the database.
A day written YYYY-MM-DD (Postgres date): not an instant, never converted through a time zone.
An instant with a time and a zone (Postgres timestamptz), shown as the local calendar date of that instant.
The point where money or dates enter or leave the app as text: display and input. Formatting and parsing happen only there.
Postgres policies deciding which rows each user may read or change. The only access control of the app.
The state after a password-recovery link signed a user in: they must choose a new password before using the app. Tied to that exact sign-in.
A link Supabase Auth sends by email (sign-up confirmation, password recovery, email change) that brings the user back to the app with a session or an error.
Email-link tokens kept for one tab (sessionStorage, never a URL) after their check failed for a transient reason, so a reload retries.
The identity of one sign-in: the session_id claim of the access token, or the user id when there is none.
The Supabase anon key meant for the browser. With the project URL, the only configuration that reaches the browser.
The name a user chooses at sign-up, kept in their profile.
One row per user, created on sign-up, with their display name and email.
The home page of the app: the current period at a glance.

actors.name: anonymous visitor
actors.description: Someone who is not signed in. Can sign up, sign in, follow email links and nothing else; reads and changes no data.

actors.name: signed-in user
actors.description: Anyone signed in, before or regardless of belonging to a given budget. Relative to a budget they are not a member of, they are "another user" and can see or change nothing in it.

actors.name: budget owner
actors.description: The member who created a budget. Everything a member can do, plus delete the budget, change its end date, and manage members and invitations.

actors.name: budget member
actors.description: A person who belongs to a budget, the owner included unless stated. Reads and edits everything in the budget.

actors.name: invited person
actors.description: Someone whose email address the owner invited. Sees the invitation after signing in with an account whose verified email matches, then accepts or declines it.

actors.name: Claude session
actors.description: A Claude Code session that imports transactions by running the import script of this repository. Never gets raw database access to real data.

features.title: Incomes
features.description: Versioned monthly incomes per member, one of them primary, with a weekend rule.

userStories.iWant: to add my income with its amount, pay day and weekend rule
userStories.soThat: it counts in the budget's monthly total

userStories.iWant: to change an income's terms when my salary changes
userStories.soThat: the change applies from now on and past periods stay as they were

userStories.iWant: to remove an income

features.title: Periods
features.description: Pay-day-to-pay-day periods, created on demand, with manual boundaries.

userStories.iWant: periods to run from pay day to pay day of the primary income
userStories.soThat: the salary is always day one of the period

userStories.iWant: to move a period boundary when the salary arrived on another day
userStories.soThat: public holidays do not put transactions in the wrong period

userStories.iWant: past periods to stay as they were when the primary income's terms change
userStories.soThat: history does not shift under me

features.title: Categories and expectations
features.description: Two-level categories with monthly or yearly expectations, and the amount left to assign.

userStories.iWant: to split the budget into categories and subcategories with a monthly expectation each
userStories.soThat: I know how much I plan to spend on what

userStories.iWant: to enter a yearly amount for a yearly cost
userStories.soThat: it is spread as one twelfth per month

userStories.iWant: to see the amount left to assign in a period, negative when I have assigned more than the income
userStories.soThat: every franc of the budget has a purpose

userStories.iWant: to delete a category I no longer need
userStories.soThat: it leaves the budget from now on while past periods keep it

userStories.iWant: to change a category's expectation from now on, or explicitly correct it from an earlier period
userStories.soThat: past periods stay as they were unless I fix a mistake on purpose

userStories.iWant: my save to be refused, with a message to reload, when another member changed the same thing in the meantime
userStories.soThat: I never silently overwrite their change

features.title: Transactions
features.description: Manual transactions, landing in the period that contains their date.

userStories.iWant: to record a transaction with an amount, a date and a category
userStories.soThat: spending is tracked against the budget

userStories.iWant: to add, edit or delete a transaction in a past period
userStories.soThat: late receipts still land in the right period

userStories.iWant: to record money coming back as a refund
userStories.soThat: it reduces what was spent in its category

features.title: Period progress view
features.description: Each period, the current one and past ones, tracked against its expectations, with its result.

userStories.iWant: to see how the current period is going against the expectations, with overspent categories shown as such
userStories.soThat: I can adjust before the period ends

userStories.iWant: to see a period's surplus or deficit, and each category's result
userStories.soThat: I know how the period went

userStories.iWant: to browse past periods and see the progress view of each
userStories.soThat: I can look back at how any period went

features.title: Subscriptions
features.description: Recurring charges and their next charge date.

userStories.iWant: to track subscriptions and see when each will next be charged
userStories.soThat: recurring costs do not surprise me

userStories.iWant: each subscription charge to be recorded automatically on its charge date, and to confirm from the home page that it really went through
userStories.soThat: I do not enter recurring charges by hand and still catch one that failed

userStories.iWant: to see a subscription's monthly cost as committed within its category's expectation
userStories.soThat: I see how much of the category is already spoken for

features.title: Debts
features.description: Debts with planned payments, their evolution and expected end date.

userStories.iWant: to record a debt with its principal, interest rate and planned monthly payment
userStories.soThat: I can follow it down to zero

userStories.iWant: payments linked to a debt to reduce what remains, interest to be added to it, and to see its history and expected end date
userStories.soThat: I know when it will be paid off, or that it never will at this pace

userStories.iWant: to adjust a debt's balance by hand
userStories.soThat: it matches my bank statement

features.title: Period comparison
features.description: Comparing periods in charts. Browsing a past period and its progress view is part of step 3 (F-PROGRESS).

userStories.iWant: to compare the income, spending and result of the last 12 periods in a chart
userStories.soThat: I see how our spending evolves

userStories.iWant: to see the spending per category across periods
userStories.soThat: I see which categories grow or shrink

userStories.iWant: to put two periods side by side
userStories.soThat: I see exactly what changed between them

features.title: Import
features.description: Bulk import of transactions from PDF bank and card statements, from CSV, or by a Claude session, through one database function.

userStories.iWant: to paste or upload a CSV of transactions
userStories.soThat: I do not type them one by one

userStories.iWant: to import transactions by running the import script of this repository with an import token
userStories.soThat: a member can delegate the import without giving Claude raw database access

userStories.iWant: imported transactions to be marked to review until I confirm them, categorised from saved merchant rules, and to save a new rule in one click when I categorise one
userStories.soThat: I check them quickly and categorisation improves over time

userStories.iWant: to create import tokens for one budget in Settings, and revoke them
userStories.soThat: I control what a Claude session can do, and can stop it at any time

userStories.iWant: to edit the merchant-to-category rules in Settings
userStories.soThat: I can fix a rule that puts a merchant in the wrong category

userStories.iWant: to open a PDF statement of my Migros Bank account, my Migros Bank credit card or my Yuh account in the app
userStories.soThat: its transactions are imported without typing them or mapping columns

userStories.iWant: card-bill payments, transfers between my own accounts, salaries and other credits to be recognised when I import a statement
userStories.soThat: nothing is counted twice and I decide what each credit is

features.title: Accounts and money flow
features.description: Accounts, planned transfers after payday, a per-period checklist and the money flow diagram.

userStories.iWant: to define my accounts and the transfers planned between them after payday
userStories.soThat: the money goes where it should every period

userStories.iWant: a per-period checklist of the manual transfers
userStories.soThat: I do not forget one

userStories.iWant: a diagram of the planned flow of money
userStories.soThat: I see the whole plan at a glance

userStories.iWant: to link a planned transfer to a category, so that its transaction is created when it is done
userStories.soThat: savings, third pillar or tax transfers count in the budget without being entered twice

rules.statement: An edit form or removal confirmation reads its record by id, never from a list, and saves over the version it opened. When another member changes a field it shows (the save is refused, or a later read shows it), it says so with their values field by field: with nothing typed it takes their version; with something typed it keeps what was typed and lets the user load their version or keep theirs, and keeping theirs saves only the fields they edited. Values that only mean something together (a category's amount and cadence, an income's pay day and weekend rule) are one field throughout: an edit to any part keeps and sends the whole group as the form shows it, and a group not edited takes the other member's version whole (D-160). The note that the form took their version goes once the user types or saves. A change to fields it does not show (the user's own save in another form, another member's change elsewhere) is taken silently. A record deleted meanwhile is said to be gone and cannot be saved; a category ended meanwhile is said to be removed, and one turned into a group meanwhile is said so and only its name can still be saved, with the typed amount named so it is not lost silently.

decisions.title: Infomaniak static hosting with an .htaccess SPA fallback

decisions.title: Periods are numbered; versions refer to period numbers
decisions.decision: Periods are numbered per budget (seq 1, 2, ...). Income validity (first_seq, end_seq) and versions (effective_from_seq) refer to seq, not to dates. An income counts in period p when first_seq <= p and (end_seq is null or p < end_seq), at the version with the greatest effective_from_seq <= p.
decisions.why: Moving a period boundary never changes which version applies.

decisions.title: Not found, never forbidden
decisions.decision: A request for a budget, income, period or invitation the caller cannot see is answered as not found; reads of rows outside one's budgets return no rows, never an error.
decisions.why: Non-members cannot tell a budget they may not see from one that does not exist.

decisions.title: Limits
decisions.decision: At most 20 owned budgets per user, 20 members per budget, 20 pending invitations per budget, 50 incomes per budget (ended ones included). Income amounts from 1 to 1 000 000 000 rappen. A budget starts at most 60 months back; an end date at most ten years ahead; a period is never empty and at most 70 days long. The limits are defined in one place in the migration.
decisions.why: Bound the work of every RPC and keep abuse cheap.

decisions.title: An income that never counted is deleted, not ended
decisions.decision: Removing an income deletes it if it never counted in a past period, and otherwise ends it from the current period. The same applies to the incomes of a member who is removed or leaves.
decisions.why: An income added by mistake leaves no trace; history is kept otherwise.

decisions.title: The primary income also blocks leaving
decisions.decision: A member whose income is the primary income can neither be removed nor leave until another income is made primary.
decisions.why: The budget must keep a primary income.

decisions.title: An end date snaps forward to a period end
decisions.decision: Setting an end date moves it forward to the end of the period that contains it, projected with the primary income's current terms. Clearing it resumes period generation. An end date that would delete existing periods is refused, and a boundary that is the budget's end date is changed through the end date.
decisions.why: The end date always falls on a period boundary without deleting history.

decisions.title: One period per calendar month
decisions.decision: Each period belongs to one calendar month (periods.month) and starts on that month's salary (anchor_date, the scheduled actual pay date). Consecutive periods have consecutive months. A period's projected end is the day before the actual pay date of the next month's nominal pay day under the terms in force for the next period. A mid-period change of the primary's pay day or weekend rule therefore applies to the next month's pay date.
decisions.why: An early salary, a close-by nominal date or a pay-day change could otherwise cut a period short and count a month's salary twice.
rejected: Projecting the end from the first pay date after the period start: an early salary created a 2-day period and a second salary in the same month (review finding 1).

decisions.title: No period starts after today
decisions.decision: Periods exist only up to the one containing today. Moving the boundary before the latest period to today or later means the salary has not arrived yet: the latest period is removed and the previous one is current again with that end. Moving any earlier boundary to today or later is refused.
decisions.why: A future period made an earlier one current again and let an edit be written to a closed period while the next one kept stale terms (review finding 2).

decisions.title: Periods are salary to salary; stored periods are facts
decisions.decision: A period runs from one salary to the day before the next. Stored periods are facts: only the boundary operations move a stored boundary. The schedule (the primary income's pay day and weekend rule) only predicts the next pay date. Structural invariants only, none depending on terms: contiguous, non-overlapping, none starting after today or after the budget's end date, each 7 to 92 days long. Known limits of the model: a first salary arriving 8 to 14 days after a period started is skipped by the projection until recorded by hand (record_early_pay_date); two salaries closer than 7 days cannot be separate periods.
decisions.why: The month anchor and the 14-day rule (D-060, D-061) tied stored periods to the terms currently in force: budgets got stuck (every period call failing) and real pay-day changes, such as from the 5th to the 25th within one month, could not be represented.
rejected: One period per calendar month within 14 days of its scheduled salary (D-060, D-061): see why.

decisions.title: The projection rule
decisions.decision: The next pay date after a period is the first actual pay date, under the primary income's terms in force, at least 15 days after the period's start; the projected end is the day before. When re-projecting because terms changed, the next pay date must also be after today, so the current period stays current. One pure function (private.next_salary_date).
decisions.why: Periods generated this way are never shorter than 15 days, an early salary never creates a stub, and a change of terms never closes a period retroactively.

decisions.title: Boundary operations, each with an inverse
decisions.decision: Four operations: set_expected_pay_date (the current period's end, after today; null resets it to the projection); record_early_pay_date (the salary arrived early: the next period starts on a date up to today); reopen_previous_period (the salary has not arrived yet: the latest period is merged into the previous one, which ends before a future date or at its projection; the inverse of an early close); move_period_start (moves the boundary between two existing periods to a date up to today; undone by moving it back). Every write RPC catches the periods up to today first. The length bounds are the abuse limit.
decisions.why: Each real-life case has one clear operation, and each has an inverse.
rejected: One move_period_boundary operation whose meaning depended on the period's position: hard to use and to undo.

decisions.why: A change made "now" must always be in force now; the discard-later-versions mechanism (D-064) is no longer needed.

decisions.title: Categories end like incomes; expectations are versioned like incomes
decisions.decision: Deleting a category that has transactions or has counted in a past period ends it from the current period and keeps it in past periods, like incomes (D-030); one that has neither is deleted. Category expectations are versioned like incomes: an edit applies from the current period, with the same optional "correct an earlier period" (D-065). Decided by the product owner on 2026-11-16.

decisions.title: Subscription cadences and charge dates
decisions.decision: Subscription cadences are monthly, quarterly, half-yearly and yearly. A subscription has a first charge date and then repeats on the same day of the month, clamped to the month's length. No weekend rule applies to subscriptions. Decided by the product owner on 2026-11-16.

decisions.decision: On its charge date, a subscription's transaction is created automatically, marked as coming from the subscription, and can be edited or deleted. The dashboard shows a notification for each such automatic charge asking the user to confirm that it really went through; until confirmed it is marked as awaiting confirmation. The user can instead say it did not go through, which removes it. Assumption (not asked of the product owner): a charge awaiting confirmation counts in totals immediately, like imported transactions (D-118). Decided by the product owner on 2026-11-16.

decisions.title: Remaining amount, interest and expected end of a debt
decisions.decision: A debt's remaining amount is the principal plus accrued interest minus the payments linked to it. When the debt has an interest rate, once per period one twelfth of the yearly rate is applied to the remaining balance and added to it, and shown in the debt's history. The expected end date is projected from the planned monthly payment; when the payment does not cover the interest, the app says the debt never ends. A manual "adjust balance" entry lets the user match their bank statement. Decided by the product owner on 2026-11-16.

decisions.title: In a merge, the merged period always wins
decisions.decision: When the latest period is merged into the previous one, everything keyed to the merged (later) period is re-keyed to the previous one and replaces what the previous period had for the same record, whatever the write times. So the terms in force before a reopen are still in force after it. Nothing is ever keyed beyond the latest period. One shared mechanism (private.rekey_period over private.period_keyed_tables). What the reopened period loses can be listed beforehand (preview_reopen). The inverse of a reopen (record_early_pay_date with the original date) restores the boundary only: what was recorded in the merged period then belongs to the reopened period, and moving it back needs explicit corrections.
decisions.why: "The later write wins" let a correction of the previous period, written after a raise in the new period, undo the raise; re-keyed versions got fresh write times and beat later corrections (review finding 1).
rejected: The later write wins (D-083).

decisions.title: What a period-keyed table must provide
decisions.decision: A table registers in private.period_keyed_tables, checked at registration: all need id uuid and budget_id uuid; validity tables first_seq integer, end_seq integer, a text name column and a check allowing end_seq = first_seq; version tables an entity column (uuid) referencing a registered validity table, effective_from_seq integer and a unique constraint on (entity, effective_from_seq). In a merge, a validity row that would never be in force is deleted, or kept as a void row (end_seq = first_seq, never in force) when other rows reference it, so a reopen never fails on a foreign key.
decisions.why: Step 3 registers categories, which transactions reference; the merge must neither fail at reopen time nor silently need columns nobody documented (review finding 4).

decisions.title: Concurrent edits: one revision per record
decisions.decision: Every editable record (budget, income, category, transaction, and every later one) has an integer revision, raised by a trigger whenever its row changes and explicitly when a dependent row changes (an income's terms, a category's expectation). Every edit or removal RPC takes p_expected_revision and refuses with record_changed when it differs; the write RPCs take the budget lock first, so a second save waits for the first and then sees the new revision. Step 3 RPCs require it (invalid_revision when missing). decisions.title: Edit forms read their record by id and compare what they show
decisions.decision: Every edit form and removal confirmation reads its record by id (useRecord), independently of the list, filter or page it was opened from, and keeps the version it opened (useEditBase) whose revision it sends. The record's revision is its one revision source, but a form compares only the fields it shows: a newer revision that leaves them as they were becomes its base in silence (the user's own save in another form, another member changing another field). When a shown field changed: with nothing typed the form takes the other version and says what changed; with something typed it lists the other member's values field by field and offers "Load their version" or "Keep mine", which keeps only the fields the user edited (react-hook-form's dirty fields) so the save sends only those. A record deleted meanwhile is said to be gone. Built once (src/hooks/use-edit-base.ts, src/hooks/use-concurrent-form.ts, src/components/changed-elsewhere.tsx, src/features/budgets/record-queries.ts) and used by incomes, the budget's name and end date, categories and transactions; steps 4 to 7 reuse it.
decisions.why: The first version looked the record up in whatever list was loaded (a transaction moved to another period by another member read as a dead end), compared revisions only (saving one settings form flagged the other) and, after "Keep mine", sent every field, reverting the other member's untouched changes. D-124 asks to refuse the second save; reloading the form would lose what was typed, and silently retrying would overwrite the other member.
rejected: Looking the record up in the loaded list.
Comparing revisions only.
"Keep mine" sending every field of the form.
Reloading the form with the other version, discarding what was typed.

decisions.title: Interest at period creation; the projection and "never"
decisions.decision: Interest is applied when a new period is created, on the balance at that moment, as one twelfth of the yearly rate rounded half up to the rappen, as an entry of that period in the debt's history (dated at the period's start). It is applied exactly once per debt and period however the period came to exist (roll-over, catch-up over several periods, an early salary), and a reopen that merges a period removes the interest entry that period created. No interest on a balance of zero or less. A planned payment less than or equal to one period's interest means the debt never ends. The projection has a horizon of 600 periods (50 years) beyond which it answers "never". Decided by the project coordinator on 2026-11-16, on the product owner's instruction to proceed on the coordinator's defaults.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-055. Periods run salary to salary, so the period, not the calendar month, is the step of interest; tying the entry to its period keeps a reopen exact.

decisions.title: Subscriptions and debts are versioned like incomes; ending follows the established rule
decisions.decision: A subscription's terms (price, cadence, category, schedule) and a debt's terms (interest rate, planned monthly payment) are versioned like incomes and category amounts, through the registry (private.period_keyed_tables), so committed figures and projections for past periods use the terms in force then, and a reopen treats them like any other recorded change. Ending or deleting follows the established rule: something that has counted in the past is ended from now and kept in the past; something that never counted is deleted. A debt with linked payments, or a subscription with charges, is never silently destroyed (a reopen keeps it as a void row). Decided by the project coordinator on 2026-11-16, on the product owner's instruction to proceed on the coordinator's defaults.
decisions.why: One mechanism for every versioned record; the user's history is never lost to a removal or a reopen.

decisions.title: A charge is a transaction with its scheduled date and a review state
decisions.decision: An automatic charge is an ordinary expense transaction linked to its subscription, with the scheduled date it was created for (charge_date, unique per subscription; the transaction's own date may be edited) and review_state 'awaiting_confirmation' until a member confirms it (confirm_subscription_charge). "Did not go through" (dismiss_subscription_charge) deletes it; delete_transaction does the same. Editing a charge keeps it a charge and does not confirm it. The column review_state is the one step 6 planned for imports (D-118), which adds its own value.
decisions.why: A charge must count in totals at once (D-109) and be edited like any transaction (R-SUBSCRIPTION-074): it is one. A single review state serves both automatic charges and, later, imports.
rejected: A separate table of charges pointing at transactions: two records for one fact.

decisions.title: A subscription counts from its first period
decisions.decision: A subscription is in force from the period it is created in (or, as an explicit correction, from an earlier one); its charges are the scheduled dates on or after its first charge date in the periods where it is in force, so creating it creates at once, awaiting confirmation, the charges of its first period up to today (for a back-dated one, those of the earlier periods too). Dates before its first period are never charged. When the budget is at its transaction limit, charges wait (the watermark stops before the first that does not fit) and are created once there is room.
decisions.why: A first charge date in the past sets the schedule without flooding closed periods with charges the user may have recorded by hand; an explicit correction is the only way to add charges to closed periods. Waiting at the limit never loses a charge.
rejected: Charging every date since the first charge date, back to the budget's start.
Skipping charges that do not fit the limit.

decisions.title: Links: payments are expenses in the debt's category
decisions.decision: A transaction is linked through add_transaction (p_debt_id or p_subscription_id) or link_transaction (which also unlinks; unlinking a charge makes it an ordinary confirmed transaction). update_transaction keeps the link. A linked transaction is an expense; a debt payment is in the debt's category; the debt or subscription is in force in the period of the date; a linked transaction keeping its period and category keeps its link even when the debt's category changed or it ended (as D-159). A refund is never a payment.
decisions.why: Step 3 callers of update_transaction send every field; a link they do not know of must not be dropped. Payments in the debt's category keep the category's spending and the debt's payments the same money.
rejected: Refunds linked to a debt as reversed payments.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 4, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Debt principal, balance adjustments and corrections
decisions.decision: A debt's principal can change only while it has no payment, interest or adjustment (a typo at creation); afterwards the balance is adjusted. adjust_debt_balance takes the balance the bank shows and the database stores the difference as a dated entry (no entry when there is none), so a payment recorded meanwhile cannot make it wrong; an adjustment can be deleted. A correction of a debt's terms from an earlier period records the terms for those periods and the projection, and never recomputes interest already added (each entry records the rate and balance it used); a wrong past interest is fixed with an adjustment. Ending a debt keeps its remaining amount. A debt created from an earlier period (a correction) starts its history at that period's start and gets no interest for periods that already existed.
decisions.why: Interest entries are facts of the moment a period was created; recomputing them could not reproduce that moment.
rejected: Recomputing every later interest entry after a rate correction.
source: owner-request: database developer decision for step 4, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Categories in use by subscriptions and debts
decisions.decision: end_category refuses (category_in_use) a category that a subscription or debt in force from that period still uses; one that any subscription version or debt references is ended rather than deleted, like one with transactions. Adding the first subcategory to a category with subscriptions or debts needs "Other", and moves them there with its transactions and expectations (create_category redefined). category_overview gains in_use and accounts for the references in removal_deletes.
decisions.why: Otherwise a removal would fail on a foreign key, a charge would land on a category not in force or on a group, or a debt's payments would have nowhere to go.
rejected: Ending the subscriptions and debts with the category.

decisions.title: Limits for subscriptions and debts
decisions.decision: Per budget at most 50 subscriptions in force and 200 in all, 50 debts in force and 200 in all (void rows not counted), and 5000 balance adjustments; prices, principals and planned payments up to 1 000 000 000 rappen; interest rates 0 to 100 % with three decimals; a schedule date at most ten years ahead; a debt's balance never grows beyond 1 000 000 000 000 rappen through interest or an adjustment. Automatic charges count towards the 50 000 transactions (D-153). Defined in one place in the step 4 migration.
decisions.why: Abuse bounds: with 50 monthly subscriptions, ten years of absence create 6000 charges in one catch-up, within the hosted statement timeout.

decisions.title: The payoff projection
decisions.decision: debt_overview projects, for a debt in force in a budget with a current period: 'paid_off' when nothing remains; otherwise the planned payment still due in the current period (the planned payment minus what was paid in it) is paid first, then each later period adds its interest and receives the planned payment, until nothing remains ('ends', with payments_left and expected_end_date, the projected end of the period of the last payment, future periods following the primary income's schedule) or the planned payment does not exceed a period's interest or the horizon is reached ('never').
decisions.why: Counting this period's payment once, whether or not it was made yet, keeps the end date stable through the period.

decisions.title: Charts: shadcn chart (Recharts), theme colours, lazy route

The page that draws a chart is its own lazily loaded route, so Recharts never reaches the first load. A debt's chart is a step line of the balance on a time axis (dates spaced by days, no time zone), its value axis scaled to the balances so a few payments show (zero drawn when in range).

decisions.title: What the subscription form previews
decisions.decision: The form asks the database for the dates (subscription_charge_dates) of the schedule it describes: a new subscription from its first charge date, starting at the period it counts from, the dates up to today flagged as charged at once; an edit with a new next charge date from that date; a new cadence alone, from now, from the current next charge date; otherwise the current schedule from its next charge. The next charge date of an edit is optional (blank keeps the schedule) and, from now, must be after today.

decisions.title: Changing a transaction's debt link takes several calls
decisions.decision: update_transaction never changes a link (D-177), so an edit that changes the debt a transaction pays calls link_transaction to remove the old link before the fields change, update_transaction, then link_transaction to add the new one, each with the revision the previous call returned. They are not one transaction: a failure part-way leaves the steps already done (the form shows the error, the lists are read again).
decisions.why: Removing first and linking last keeps every intermediate state valid (a payment is always in its debt's category). Q-111 asks for one call.

decisions.title: Answering an automatic charge
decisions.decision: A charge awaiting confirmation is answered from the dashboard card or from the transactions list. "It went through" confirms at once; "It did not go through" asks first and says the charge will not be created again for that date. When another member answered first (record_changed, or the charge is gone), the list is read again and a message says so; nothing is resent.
decisions.why: Dismissing deletes a transaction for good (R-SUBSCRIPTION-077); confirming is harmless.

decisions.title: The debt chart: one point per date, round ticks, few marks
decisions.decision: The chart draws one point per date (the balance after its last event) on to today; its tooltip lists every event of the date with its amount and resulting balance. Value ticks are round (1, 2, 2.5 or 5 times a power of ten rappen, with rappen shown when needed); time ticks fall on month or year starts beyond three months. Beyond 24 dates only balance adjustments are marked (interest comes every period and would bury the line); the opening is a hollow square, a payment a dot. The history table shows the latest 12 events until all are asked for. A debt with only its opening shows a sentence instead. The chart is one named image, not a keyboard stop; the table is its text.

decisions.title: Interest on the balance before the period, at period creation; the projection and "never"
decisions.decision: A period's interest for a debt is computed when the period is created, on the debt's balance from everything dated before the period's start (its opening, payments, adjustments and earlier interest), whatever day the catch-up runs, as one twelfth of the yearly rate rounded half up to the rappen, as an entry of that period in the debt's history (dated at the period's start). A debt whose opened_on is not before the period's start gets no interest for that period; its first comes with the next one, so the history always starts with the opening. It is computed once: a payment or adjustment back-dated later does not recompute it (an adjustment exists for that). It is applied exactly once per debt and period however the period came to exist; a reopen that merges a period removes its entry and creating the period again computes it by the same rule, so redoing without other changes gives the same amount. No interest on a balance of zero or less. A planned payment less than or equal to one period's interest means the debt never ends; the projection has a horizon of 600 periods (50 years). Supersedes D-172.
decisions.why: Re-review finding 4: interest on the balance at the moment of the catch-up gave an entry dated before the opening (an early pay date) and a different amount for a period created again after a payment dated inside it. The projection already assumes this rule (each period's interest on what remains after the previous period).
rejected: The balance at the moment of creation: depends on the day the catch-up runs.

decisions.title: One import, in batches of idempotent chunks
decisions.decision: private.import_plan decides what each row does and private.import_apply does it; preview_import, import_transactions, import_with_token and import_skipped_anyway all use them. A batch has an id the caller generates and up to 100 chunks of up to 500 rows (50 000 rows); a chunk sent again answers as the first time and records nothing. A chunk is all or nothing, refused before anything is written when the transaction limit cannot hold it (detail: how many would fit).

A rule holds a fragment and a category and matches a key that contains it; the longest matching fragment wins; a rule whose category is not in force on a row's date does not apply to it. The one-click offer proposes the transaction's whole key; Settings can shorten it. A category's first subcategory moves its rules to Other; deleting a category deletes its rules.

decisions.title: Import tokens (revised)
decisions.decision: A member creates a token for one budget with a name and an expiry (30 days by default, at most a year); the secret (bti_ and 244 random bits) is answered once and only its SHA-256 is stored. At most 10 tokens that can still be used a budget; a revoked or expired one can be deleted, and those kept are pruned to the newest 20 and 365 days. import_with_token is the only function callable without a session, by POST only (a GET is refused with read_only_call before the token is looked at). An unknown, expired or revoked token, or one whose creator left, was removed or deleted their account, gets invalid_token after one index lookup, before any lock or catch-up. A call never waits for another token call: the same token busy, or every slot for token work taken, answers token_busy or imports_busy at once, doing nothing and counting nothing (D-453). Every call that does work counts, whatever its outcome, cancelled included: 60 calls and 5000 rows within any 60 minutes, 300 calls and 20 000 rows within any 24 hours (by whole minutes: a call counts 60 to 61 minutes and 24 hours to 24 hours and 1 minute, D-463), checked and counted in one step under the token's lock; a refusal after the count is answered in the error column, not raised. A token call takes at most 250 rows. The batch records the token, never the caller. Batches, skipped rows and remembered choices are read through paged functions only.
decisions.why: The step 6 review: a refused call must cost the attacker too, parallel calls must not pass the limit together, fixed hourly windows let twice the limit through at the boundary, tokens must not pile up, and a token in a URL ends up in logs.
rejected: Counting only successful calls: free probing.
Fixed clock-hour windows.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16
code: supabase/migrations/20261119100000_import.sql

decisions.title: What a token is told
decisions.decision: A token's answer does not depend on the budget's content: every argument is checked before anything of the budget, "to categorise" is created under its fixed name (the token cannot name it), and a token is never told how many rows would fit. Coarse states still reach it, because a script must be able to say why nothing was imported: the budget is nearly full (transaction_limit_reached, refused whenever it has room for fewer than 250 transactions, D-451), the budget is far behind (catching_up), its import storage of the day is used up (import_limit_reached, D-452), and its lock was held for more than a second (budget_busy, D-453).
decisions.why: Answer to Q-191 and the step 6 review (F1): any budget-dependent difference is an oracle on the budget's transactions.
rejected: Hiding the two coarse states: the script could not explain a refusal.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16
code: supabase/migrations/20261119100000_import.sql

decisions.title: Duplicates are counted per batch
decisions.decision: Rows of one batch are never duplicates of each other. A row is compared with every existing transaction of the same kind, whatever its origin: the same bank transaction id, else the same date, amount and description, either as the transaction is now or as it was first imported. Each existing transaction absorbs at most one row of the batch, counted over all its chunks, whatever order they arrive in and however often one is sent again; the same statement imported twice imports nothing the second time. Import anyway is per row or for all skipped rows of a batch.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F4, F17): counting per chunk let a statement split in two chunks import a duplicate, and editing an imported transaction made the same line import again.
source: owner-request: coordinator review of the step 6 database (import), 2026-11-16
code: supabase/migrations/20261119100000_import.sql

decisions.title: Possible matches: nearest date, once per batch
decisions.decision: A row is a possible match of an existing transaction of the same kind that was not imported (typed, or a charge), with the same amount and a date within three days either way; descriptions are not compared. Each existing transaction goes to the row nearest in date (ties: the earlier row, then a charge awaiting confirmation) and absorbs at most one row of the batch. Default: skip the row; when the match is a charge awaiting confirmation the import confirms it and the preview says so; the member can import the row anyway. The batch counts its matched rows. With a token, matches are skipped and left for the member.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-192: bank descriptions rarely look like what a member typed, so comparing them would miss most matches; the nearest date is the likeliest pair.
rejected: Matching only when the descriptions look alike.

decisions.title: Confirming a frozen import
decisions.decision: Confirming an imported transaction changes no amount, date, category or link, so it is allowed on a frozen transaction (a payment of an ended debt).
decisions.why: Undo keeps frozen transactions (D-379); the member must still be able to empty the review.

decisions.title: "To categorise" is the import's place only
decisions.decision: Each budget gets, at its first import that needs it, one top-level category flagged as its "to categorise" place (the name the member passes, a fixed name for a token; from the first period; created even at the category limits). Only imported transactions still to review can be in it: no hand-typed transaction, subscription, debt, planned transfer or merchant rule uses it, and it does not count toward the 200 categories in force. It is renamable, has no expectation, takes no subcategory, cannot end while it holds transactions, and a transaction in it cannot be confirmed. my_budgets names it only while it is in force; category_overview flags it.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-190 and the step 6 review (F12): it is a waiting room, not a category to plan with.

decisions.title: One cleaner for free text
decisions.decision: Every name and description of every step goes through one helper: control characters and bidirectional or zero-width formatting characters are removed, every other run of white space becomes one space, and the result is trimmed, before validation and before any comparison. An import's details are stored normalised the same way. Markup and spreadsheet formulas stay as text: the screens escape them, and an export must neutralise them.
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F13): the same text must compare equal wherever it came from, and invisible characters must not hide what a name says.

decisions.title: A salary credit (revised)
decisions.decision: A credit is a salary credit when the source says so (hint salary) or when its amount equals an income's amount and its date is within five days either side of a period start: on or after the start of its own period, or before the start of the next period (projected when it does not exist yet), at the income's amount in force in that period. It is skipped by default; imported anyway it is extra income. A different amount changes nothing by itself; the preview shows the planned amount beside the row's.

decisions.title: Refused rows are stored bounded
decisions.decision: Of a row that was not imported, only its known keys are kept, each within its limit, and only the names of unknown keys; a call whose rows argument exceeds 2 MB is refused whole (invalid_rows) before any row is read; the request body itself is read and parsed before the function runs, so what bounds it there is the gateway (not verified for the hosted project: Q-280).
decisions.why: The step 6 review (F3): a stolen token could otherwise store megabytes of arbitrary JSON per call.

decisions.title: Ending a transfer keeps what was done
decisions.decision: Only a member's act deletes a transfer's transaction: undoing "done", marking an automatic transfer not done, or deleting the transaction. Ending a transfer removes its occurrences from that period on but keeps every mark already made and every transaction link; a period's checklist lists the transfers in force plus those with a mark or a transaction there, flagged as ended (is_ended); preview_end_transfer answers only the outcome or the refusal. The one exception is a reopen (D-382).

decisions.title: The merchant key's cases

Otherwise it goes: one made by the catch-up with its transaction (made again if the period comes back, like a debt's interest), a member's leaving its transaction as an ordinary one. decisions.title: Averages over the completed periods, and a category's own average
decisions.decision: An average is the sum over the completed periods of the range divided by their number, rounded to the rappen with halves away from zero (also for a negative result); null when none is completed. The average result is the average of the results, so it can differ by a rappen from the average income minus the average spent. A category's average spent divides by every completed period of the range (so the categories' averages add up to the trend's); beside it, active_average_spent divides by active_count, the completed periods of the range in which the category was in force or had spending (null when that count is 0), for a category that started or stopped inside the range.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-160 (coordinator decision): Daycare, CHF 800 in each of its 3 periods of 11, showed an average of 218.18.
rejected: Replacing the average over the whole range: the lines would no longer add up to the trend.

decisions.title: Interest and moved boundaries (revised)
decisions.decision: D-272 holds as a statement about the stored data after any change of a period's boundaries: a period's interest entry exists only for a debt opened before the period's start. A start may not move to on or before the opening of a debt that has an interest entry in that period: the change is refused with interest_before_opening and nothing is removed (D-467; a trigger on the period's start, so every boundary operation is covered); preview_move_period_start gives that refusal, and its interest_removed is always 0. The other way, a start moved later so that a debt is now opened before the start of a period without an entry, adds nothing: interest is computed once, when the period is created, on the balance before its start, and computing it afterwards would charge a period that began, as recorded, before the debt existed, on a balance that already includes later rows.
decisions.why: The step 5 review (M1): a moved start put a period's interest before the debt's opening, so the history began with interest.
rejected: Adding the interest when a start moves later: a retroactive charge on a balance that is no longer the one before the start.

decisions.title: Far behind, only the catch-up calls work
decisions.decision: A call other than ensure_periods and get_current_period answers catching_up at once, before the budget lock and without any work, when the budget's last period ended more than 62 days before today (or its end date); within that it does its own roll-over as before. Only ensure_periods and get_current_period (and create_budget, for its first periods) do multi-period work, one step per call (at most 120 periods and about two seconds), however often the catch-up is called within one statement. They wait at most two seconds for a lock another session holds, then answer catching_up, so the client's loop tries again and never meets the statement timeout. Supersedes D-270 (whose bound and step stay).
decisions.why: The step 5 review (S1, S5): a refused call did a whole step under the lock and discarded it, so six calls at once ran into the 8 s timeout, ensure_periods included; clearing the end date of a long-ended budget did two steps in one call.

decisions.title: A retried add records once
decisions.decision: add_transaction, add_income, create_category, create_subscription, create_debt, create_account and create_transfer take an optional p_client_id (a uuid the client generates once per user action and sends with every retry). The first call records the id with the ids of the rows it created (kept 7 days); the same id sent again by the same member, for the same budget, the same call and the same arguments, creates nothing and answers those rows as they are now (none if deleted since). The same id from another member, for another budget, another call or other arguments is refused with request_reused before anything is written, and the refusal says nothing about the first request. The check runs under the budget lock, so a double click waits for the first call and answers its rows. Retries of the other writes are already harmless: edits, ends, marks (mark_transfer_done) and balance adjustments (adjust_debt_balance) name the revision they read and answer record_changed on a retry; an import chunk is idempotent by batch and chunk.
decisions.why: Answer to Q-090 (coordinator decision): a lost answer made the screen say nothing was saved, the user saved again, and the transaction was recorded twice.
rejected: Overwriting or returning another member's record for a reused id.

decisions.title: Rounded figures are checked within 0.05
decisions.decision: Where a statement prints a product it rounds (an amount times an exchange rate, a processing fee as a percentage, a CHF amount charged abroad plus its fee), the parser accepts the printed figure when it differs from the exact product by less than CHF 0.05; a securities quantity times its price must give the amount within one unit of the quantity's last decimal times the price, plus one rappen. Every sum, subtotal, carried-forward line, total and running balance must match exactly.
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-088 asks for the arithmetic the statement prints to be checked, but the banks' rounding rules are not known (Q-205): every CHF figure of the card-bill sample is a multiple of 0.05, and one row differs from its printed parts by 0.02. A bound below 0.05 accepts any rounding to 0.05 (nearest, up or down) and still refuses a misread digit.
rejected: Requiring exact products, which refuses real statements.
Not checking rates and fees, which lets a misread rate through.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Unknown entry types are kept, malformed known ones refused
decisions.decision: Inside a statement the parser recognises, an entry of a type it does not know (a cash withdrawal, an interest or fee line, a Yuh sale ...) is kept with its printed text as description and the default of its direction; a hint is added only from a leading label (Retrait, Intérêt, Frais ...). An entry that starts like a known type (Achat, Débit TWINT, Paiement, a Yuh Achat with security lines) but does not match its pattern refuses the statement, as does any item outside the table's columns or any amount the parser cannot explain.
decisions.why: The samples show few entry types; refusing every statement with a new type would make the import useless, while the column totals and balances still prove that every unknown entry has the right amount (R-IMPORT-088). A known type that does not match is a sign the layout changed.
rejected: Refusing a statement with any unknown entry type.
Skipping lines the parser does not understand.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: pdf.js loaded on demand, fetching nothing
decisions.decision: Statements are read with pdfjs-dist 6.4.299, the version the fixtures were captured with, imported dynamically on the first read so that the main bundle does not grow. Its worker is a same-origin file emitted by the build (production CSP: script-src 'self', worker-src 'self' blob:). No CMap, standard font, ICC profile or wasm decoder is configured or fetched (fetching in the worker and wasm are off), fonts are not installed into the page, and the bytes are passed in memory. Files above 10 MB or 50 pages are refused before or right after opening.
decisions.why: D-127 keeps the file in the browser; fetching resources from a CDN would leak that a statement is being read and break the CSP. Bank statements embed their fonts and need none of these resources for their text. Monthly statements are a few pages and well under 1 MB, so the bounds leave a wide margin while stopping a hostile file early.
rejected: Bundling pdf.js in the main chunk.
Loading the worker or resources from a CDN.
A newer pdf.js than the fixtures were captured with.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Parsers return codes and data; the screens own the words
decisions.decision: A parse returns the recognised source, what identifies the statement (its period or bill date), one entry per transaction with codes (direction, hint, proposed handling) and the extra data, the controls it checked, and the full source-specific document in the shape of the fixtures' expected.json. A refusal is a typed reason with its figures (the control, the printed and computed amounts) or the line it could not read. The English notes of expected.json (handling.why, skipped.reason) are kept for the fixture comparison as developer notes; the screens translate the codes, never these notes.
decisions.why: The screens are bilingual (R-I18N) and R-IMPORT-100 compares the parse with expected.json exactly.
rejected: Returning user-facing messages from the parsers.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: An own transfer needs the holder's name and address
decisions.decision: A payment or standing order on the Migros Bank account, and a transfer received on Yuh, is flagged as a transfer between the owner's own accounts when the counterparty's name has the same words as the holder's name (in either order) and its street and town lines equal the holder's address, compared without case, punctuation or spacing (Yuh prints "Chemin du Test, 12"). The country line and the IBAN are not compared.
decisions.why: docs/import-sources.md names the name and the address as the only clues on the Migros Bank statement, and says a payment to another person at the same address is not an own transfer (Q-063). Applying the same test to Yuh keeps one rule for both and flags the sample's transfer.
rejected: The name alone, which would flag a namesake.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Any credit before the first card is the payment received
decisions.decision: On a card bill, a dated row with a trailing minus before the first card section is the payment received, whatever its label ("Votre paiement - Merci", with LSV, partial, upper case or another wording), and is skipped like it. A debit row there must be the late-payment interest or a fee, or the bill is refused.
decisions.why: Review: under any other label the payment came out as a credit to review while the bill still added up, so no control fired and the card-bill payment would have been counted twice. Matching the position and the sign, not the words, holds for every wording.
rejected: Matching the label "Votre paiement - Merci" only.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A repeated bank id identifies no transaction
decisions.decision: A bank transaction id (TWINT id, Yuh reference) printed on more than one entry of the same statement is not a transaction id: every entry carrying it gets none, and all the entries stay. This also answers whether a TWINT id can repeat: the parser does not assume it cannot.
decisions.why: With "same bank id means duplicate", a repeated id (a reversal, a split booking, a misprint) would lose a transaction; an entry without an id is still imported. Identical genuine entries with different ids keep their ids.
rejected: Keeping the id on the first entry only.
Refusing the statement.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Unknown entries described by their first line; text outside tables ignored
decisions.decision: Inside a statement the parser recognises, an entry of a type it does not know is kept, described by its first text line only (the other lines, which can name people, addresses or IBANs, stay in textLines on the device), with the default of its direction; a hint comes only from a leading label (Retrait, Intérêt, Frais ...) or from the statement's own category line, never from a word inside a merchant name. An entry that starts like a known type but does not match its pattern or its column, any item outside the table's columns, and a rotated or right-to-left item inside a table refuse the statement. Text outside the tables is ignored: page headers and footers, the lines after "Montant dû" on the card bill, and Yuh lines outside a currency table.
decisions.why: Supersedes D-331, whose wording ("any item outside the table's columns refuses") did not say that rotated items were dropped and text outside the tables ignored, and whose descriptions of unknown entries could carry a third party's address and IBAN.
rejected: Refusing a statement with any unknown entry type.
Skipping lines the parser does not understand.
The whole entry text as description.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Bounds on items, page size and time
decisions.decision: Each read has its own pdf.js worker, stopped when the read ends. A page outside 500 to 700 by 700 to 1000 pt is refused before its text is read; the text is streamed and the read stops beyond 5000 items on a page or 20 000 in the document; after 20 seconds the worker is terminated and the file refused. Lines are grouped in one pass over the items sorted by baseline. The same item and page bounds apply to a text layer given directly to the parser. A reader that cannot be loaded (offline, a release replaced its chunk) is a refusal of its own, and any other fault while reading a refusal too: the entry point never throws.
decisions.why: Review: a 425 kB PDF with one very tall page and 120 000 lines stalled the main thread for 53 s, and a 916 kB PDF inflating to 300 MB of text operators took 33 s and 1.7 GB. The real statements have at most 219 items per page and read in well under a second, so the bounds leave a wide margin.
rejected: No bounds beyond file size and page count.
Parsing in a worker of our own (the bounds make the main-thread work small).
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: Purchase dates must be plausible
decisions.decision: A purchase date after its booking date, or more than 366 days before it, refuses the statement with the control named and both dates. Value dates are not compared with purchase dates (Q-209).
decisions.why: The purchase date decides the budget period of the transaction (D-128); a misread or misprinted year would put it in a period years away while every amount still adds up.
rejected: Accepting any date.
Clamping a wrong date to the booking date.
source: owner-request: coordinator, review round of the step 6 statement parsers, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: How entries become import rows
decisions.decision: toImportBatch(statement) returns the source (migros_account, migros_card, yuh), the statement's dates (its period; for a card bill the day after the previous bill to the bill date), the rows in statement order each with its entry number beside it, the entries not sent with a code, and the adjustments made. A row has date, amount, direction, description (cut to 500 characters at a code-point boundary), merchant (200), bank_transaction_id (dropped, not cut, above 100), hint and details. Details: purchase_time, booking_date, value_date, card, original_currency with original_amount in that currency's minor unit, exchange_rate as the printed decimal string, fee in rappen, merchant_category, security (the ISIN), location (place and country code); above 2000 bytes they are dropped in this order: location, security, merchant_category, exchange_rate, original amount and currency together, fee, card, value_date, purchase_time, booking_date. An own transfer goes without description and merchant (its payee is the holder). transfer_to_person is given to a TWINT payment to a phone number only: the statements do not show whether the payee of a payment or standing order is a person.
decisions.why: The import function refuses a row with any other key or out of its bounds; shortening in a stated way and saying so keeps the import going and visible. Integers and decimal strings keep money exact.
rejected: Refusing a statement with a field too long.
Truncating ids.
Guessing persons from payee names.

decisions.title: Entries of 0.00 are shown, not imported
decisions.decision: An entry of 0.00 (a currency conversion rounded to nothing) stays in the entry list with the handling nothing-to-import, and the mapping lists it among the entries not sent, with the code zero-amount.
decisions.why: The import function refuses an amount of 0, and leaving the line out of the list would make the statement look incomplete next to the PDF.
rejected: Dropping the entry.
Sending it and letting the database refuse it.

decisions.title: An ended budget is one with an end and no current period, caught up

decisions.title: A shared comparison link opens in the viewer's current budget

decisions.title: Chart palette re-derived: all pairs apart under every colour-vision deficiency
decisions.decision: The five chart tokens are, light: #3c5296, #d06002, #0da3a8, #a668f9, #812f52 (each at least 3:1 on the white card); dark: #2265db, #df692a, #14a185, #a77fd4, #a9348d (at least 3:1 on the dark card). Chosen by a search in OKLCH and checked over all pairs (not only neighbours) by two measures: the dataviz validator (OKLab: light worst 12.0 protan/deutan, 14.4 tritan, normal vision 16.4; dark 11.0 and 9.9, normal vision 17.4; target 8, normal-vision floor 15) and the reviewer's (Machado 2009 simulation, CIE76: every pair at least 29.5 light and 22.8 dark under protan, deutan and tritan; floor 20). Lines also carry their slot's mark and dash. D-190's claim that "marks have shapes" was not true of the category chart before this change, and the earlier light tokens were 2.2 to 4.4:1 on the card; D-190 is corrected to point here.
decisions.why: Five lines can all cross, so every pair must stay apart, under deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia, in both themes; the debt chart uses the same tokens and keeps passing.

decisions.title: How a comparison chart scrolls
decisions.decision: Columns need at least 24 px per period, lines 20 px; the frame is divided into as many whole periods as fit and the content is that width times the number of periods, so scrolling to the newest end leaves no period cut at either edge. The value axis is drawn outside the frame on the chart's own ticks, with CHF at its top.
decisions.why: At 1280 px with the sidebar, 24 periods at 44 px each overflowed and the scrolled-in axis was out of view; a frame that holds whole periods never shows half of one.
rejected: Squeezing every period into the width on a phone (unreadable columns).
An axis inside the scrolling content.

decisions.title: The categories table on a phone
decisions.decision: Below the small breakpoint the sticky name column is 7 rem (112 px) wide and its name wraps to two lines; the average comes after the periods, so the first column beside the name is a whole period. Wider screens keep a 14 rem name column.
decisions.why: The 248 px name column left 6 px for figures at 320 px; the table is the chart's text alternative and must be readable there.
rejected: Dropping the sticky column on phones (the name scrolls away from its figures).
One category at a time on phones (no overview).

decisions.title: One request id per add, from the form
decisions.decision: Every add form (transaction, category, income, subscription, debt) generates one request id when it opens and sends it as p_client_id with every save; it gets a new one after a save went through (the transaction form's "save and add another" included) and after request_reused, and keeps it after a lost answer or any other refusal, so the same save sent again records once. A refusal changes nothing in the database, so keeping the id after one is safe: a corrected save with the same id is a first use. The lost-answer message now says that saving again is safe; request_reused says the values were already saved with other content and to check the list before saving again.
decisions.why: Answers Q-250 with the database's D-390. An id per request (not per form) would make a retry a new add; an id per action across edits of the values would be refused as reused, which the form then says in words.
rejected: A new id per click (a retry after a lost answer would record twice).
Keeping the id after request_reused (every later save would be refused).

decisions.title: The comparison screens take what the database now gives
decisions.decision: Side by side opens on the database's default (the last two completed periods) and says in words, under the picker, in the column heading and in the period list, which chosen side is still running (a_is_current, b_is_current). The categories view shows active_average_spent ("over the N periods it was in use") under the average where active_count differs from completed_count, and both views take "over the plan" from the database's flags. Transfers' committed figures (step 7) are read but not shown yet. The transaction form's earliest date is my_budgets.first_period_start (D-392), read with the budget's counts.
decisions.why: D-383, D-384, D-391 and D-392 give these figures; the client no longer decides them.
rejected: Hiding a running side (the user may want it, it is only marked).

decisions.title: The import page: read here, previewed under the import's own batch, sent in parts
decisions.decision: A PDF is read with readStatementFile (pdf.js and the parsers load on the first file, in chunks of their own) and mapped with toImportBatch; a CSV is mapped on the page. The client generates the batch id when the rows are ready and names it in every preview and every part. A member's choice is sent only where it differs from what the database proposes (a row's action, a credit's kind, a category in force on its date), so choices are remembered only where the member made one. The preview is asked per part of 500 rows, again 400 ms after the last change; the import is offered only once every part's answer is current, then sends the same rows. The rows are drawn 100 at a time with a filter (all, to import, skipped, invalid); the statement's extra data is in a disclosure per row. After the import: the counts from the answers, the rows not imported (list_import_skipped_rows) with "import anyway", the link to the review and undo.
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-252 and R-IMPORT-208 ask the preview to equal the write; the page must stay usable with 1200 rows on a phone.
rejected: Sending every choice explicitly (it would remember choices the member never made).
One preview call for all rows (the function takes 500).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 screens (part B, import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: An interrupted import is resumed by opening the same file
decisions.decision: While parts are sent the page asks before leaving. The batch id, the parts confirmed, the source and a SHA-256 fingerprint of the rows are kept in localStorage (never the rows: they hold bank data); after a reload the page says an import stopped after part n of m. Opening the same statement again (same fingerprint) reuses the batch id: every part is sent again and those already recorded answer as before. A finished import removes the note; "forget it" removes it by hand.
decisions.why: The rows must not be stored on the device; the import is idempotent by batch and part, so sending all parts again is safe.
rejected: Keeping the rows to resume without the file (bank data in browser storage).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 screens (part B, import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The CSV mapping
decisions.decision: The separator is detected among semicolon, comma and tab (the one that splits the first lines into equal numbers of cells, the most cells winning) and can be changed; a file that is not UTF-8 is read as Windows-1252. The header's names pre-fill the mapping for the user to check. A date format fills itself only when it alone reads every date; otherwise the user chooses among DD.MM.YYYY, DD.MM.YY, MM.DD.YYYY, DD/MM/YYYY, MM/DD/YYYY, YYYY-MM-DD and DD-MM-YYYY. Amounts: one signed column (the user says what a negative is) or money out and money in; a decimal point or comma; apostrophes, spaces or the other mark as thousands separators; a trailing minus or brackets; more than two non-zero decimals is refused, never rounded. The statement dates sent are the earliest and latest row dates. The mapping is remembered per budget and header in localStorage.
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-082; Swiss exports use semicolons, decimal commas and DD.MM.YYYY, and 03.04 is ambiguous.
rejected: Guessing day-first for ambiguous dates.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 screens (part B, import), 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The review in the transactions list
decisions.decision: A "to review" filter (review=1) and an import's filter (batch=<id>) are chips kept in the address; each imported row shows "to review" or "needs a category", a confirm button (none, with why, while in "to categorise") and the statement's data in a disclosure. Confirm all applies to the batch when one is filtered. After an edit gives an imported transaction to review a real category, the page offers "always put this merchant in this category?" with the merchant key the database computed and the number of others waiting in "to categorise" whose key contains it (read from list_transactions, up to 200); not offered when a rule's fragment is already contained in the key. One click calls create_merchant_rule with p_apply and says how many moved.
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-007, R-IMPORT-209; the database has no preview of a rule (Q-271).

decisions.title: An import token's secret stays in its dialog

The dialog says it is shown once, offers a copy button, and says to put it in the environment of the session that runs the script as BUDGET_IMPORT_TOKEN, never in a conversation (docs/import-script.md).
decisions.why: R-IMPORT-074, R-SECURITY-005.

decisions.title: "To categorise" in the screens
decisions.decision: Pickers (transaction, subscription, debt, rule) drop the categories flagged is_to_categorise from list_categories_for_date / category_overview. An import waiting there opens in the transaction form with no category chosen, so saving it gives it a real one. The budget page lists it with a mark ("Import"), "No plan", what it is for, and an edit form that changes the name only; "add a subcategory" is not offered and "remove" is disabled with the reason while it holds transactions. decisions.title: Migrations before the first deployment
decisions.decision: No database has been deployed yet. Until the first deployment, any migration file may be corrected in place, whichever step it belongs to; the first deployment freezes every migration file then present, and from then on every change is a new migration. Until that deployment the chain is guaranteed only as a whole: some files call or read what a later file creates (the step 4 file calls private.catch_up_gate, the step 5 and step 6 files read columns of the step 7 file); it is applied in one push, never as a prefix, and functions are not reordered for it (the owner's decision in the last database fix round; docs/deployment.md).
decisions.why: Fix rounds of a step under review would otherwise stack migrations that only repair code nobody has run, and the reviewed file would no longer be the one that runs.
rejected: A new migration for every fix from the start: the reviewed code and the code that runs drift apart before anything is deployed.

decisions.title: What a token learns of the room
decisions.decision: A token call is refused with transaction_limit_reached whenever the budget has room for fewer transactions than a token call's maximum rows (250), whatever rows it sends and before any planning: a token learns one bit ("nearly full"), never the count. A signed-in member keeps the exact answer (detail {"fits": n}).

rejected: Refusing only when the rows sent do not fit: an exact oracle of the room.
