decisions.title: Import storage per budget is bounded (amended: members and tokens have separate allowances)
decisions.decision: Whatever members and tokens do, a budget's import storage is bounded. Within a rolling 24 hours: 200 new batches started by members and, apart from them, 50 started by tokens; 20 000 rows submitted to a write in all, of which tokens at most 10 000 (import_limit_reached, whose detail names the limit: imports_per_day, token_imports_per_day, rows_per_day, token_rows_per_day, imports_kept); 20 tokens created, deleted ones included (token_limit_reached). Kept: 2 000 batches (at the limit, the oldest batches that hold no transaction and no skipped row any more go first; import_limit_reached when none can), the newest 20 000 skipped rows (older ones go; the batch's counts stay), the newest 50 chunk answers and none older than 7 days (a chunk whose answer is forgotten stays recorded, so sending it again answers chunk_expired and never imports it twice), and staged preview parts for a day, at most 100. Measured again with incompressible text at every limit (this round): a day adds at most about 82 MB (skipped rows 65 MB, chunk answers 15 MB, the 250 batches and their chunks 1.4 MB), and all that is kept beyond the transactions is at most about 120 MB (skipped rows 66 MB, chunk answers 19 MB, staged parts 11 MB, 2 000 batches with up to 200 000 recorded chunks about 25 MB). Amended in place in the last database fix round (the separate allowances, the detail); undoing an import gives back none of the day's allowance.
decisions.why: The re-review stored 39 MB in 7 s through chunks and recycled 30 tokens in 4.4 s: each call was bounded, nothing bounded the total. Amended: one token sent 52 one-row calls in 0.8 s and used the day's 50 new batches, locking the members out for 24 hours, and a household importing its history hit the same wall at its 51st file (re-check 3, import should-fix 1).
rejected: Refusing at the kept limits only: a stolen token could block imports for good.
Only a time-based pruning: no total bound.

decisions.title: Token calls never queue
decisions.decision: A token call never waits for another token call: another call of the same token doing work answers token_busy at once, and when the two slots for token work (all budgets together) are taken the call answers imports_busy at once; neither does any work or counts, and the script waits and sends again. A working call waits at most a second for its budget's lock (budget_busy, counted) and takes at most 250 rows (a member's call 500); with the merchant key's bounded steps and the duplicate lookup by index its database time stays far within the anon statement timeout (measured worst case about 0.3 s on a 45 000-transaction budget). Were it cancelled all the same, it answers call_cancelled and still counts. A visitor with only the publishable key can still make PostgREST read and parse a request body of any size the gateway lets through (Q-280) and receive invalid_token; every other function is refused.
decisions.why: A cancelled transaction cannot be counted, and calls of one token waiting on its lock piled up until the API stalled for every budget (re-review M-2).
rejected: Counting in a separate committed transaction (dblink): an extension and a connection per call for what bounded work and try-locks already give.
Keeping 500 rows a token call: under a 40-loop hammer on a loaded machine one call in 170 hit the statement timeout.

decisions.title: The CSV decimal mark is read from the whole file, or asked
decisions.decision: Each amount cell says a point, a comma, either (no mark: -350, 1'234) or ambiguous (one mark followed by exactly three digits, a whole part of one to three digits: 1.200, 1,200). Both marks: the last one is the decimal mark; one mark twice groups thousands. Over every amount of the mapped columns: one reading settles it for every line (ambiguous lines follow it); only "either": a point, which changes no value and is not remembered; ambiguous and nothing settling it: the member must choose, and the screen says it could not be decided, naming the lines; a point on some lines and a comma on others: the file is refused, naming those lines, and no choice reads it. A choice made on the screen wins; a mapping remembered from an earlier file keeps its mark only if the member chose it or its file settled it (remembered mappings now carry version 2; older ones lose the assumed point). Under a settled point, 1.200 reads as 1.20 (trailing zeros of three decimals were already accepted, D-444).

rejected: Refuse every three-digit fraction: a settled file would lose its readable lines.

decisions.title: Occurrences are keyed by date, not by period
decisions.decision: An occurrence of a planned transfer is identified by a date, its key, never by a period. A fixed-day transfer follows the calendar exactly like a subscription: a cadence (monthly, quarterly or yearly), a first date that sets the phase, and a nominal day clamped to the month's length, its dates computed by the subscriptions' own schedule code; each date is the key and the due date of an occurrence of the period that contains it, so a short period can have none and a long one two, and a yearly payment is one occurrence a year. A pay-date transfer has one occurrence per pay date of its income in the period: for a chosen income in force, each of its actual pay dates in the period (key = that date); otherwise (the primary income, a chosen income not in force or deleted) one occurrence keyed by the period's scheduled pay date. Every period stores the scheduled pay date of the salary that started it (periods.pay_key): the previous period's projected end plus one by the projection rule when the period is created, the first period's start for the first; a reopen deletes the merged period with its key, and recording that salary again creates the same key. A period is never without a key: when that date is already another period's, it takes the next scheduled pay date no period has (D-490); a key two periods give a transfer (switching between its chosen income and the primary one) belongs to the earlier period when both are paydays; with a fixed day they are two occurrences (amended by D-521). Marks are stored by transfer and key. Amended by D-610: a transfer naming no income has one occurrence per period, identified by the period's number; one naming an income one per scheduled pay date of that income, whichever is the primary.
decisions.why: The review (M2, M3): keyed by period, one real transfer could be recorded twice after a reopen, and short and long periods produced transactions the bank never made. A key that does not move with boundaries makes "the same occurrence" well defined across early and late salaries, reopens and boundary moves. A stored scheduled pay date is needed because the primary income's history is not versioned per period (a primary switch would otherwise change every past key).
rejected: Keying the primary income's occurrence by the period's start: a salary recorded again on another day would make a member's mark a different occurrence.
Computing the scheduled pay date from the current primary income's terms: a primary switch or a pay-day edit would move past keys and orphan marks.
Giving a colliding period the next scheduled date: every later period's key would shift by a month.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 7 occurrence model redesign, after the independent review of 747686c, 2026-11-16
owner-request: database developer decision for the step 7 occurrence model, within the coordinator's brief, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: A transfer's first counted day
decisions.decision: A transfer counts from the first day of the period it is created in, or corrected from, or that period's scheduled pay date when it is earlier (a salary that came late): transfers.starts_on. Nothing before it is planned, and a done date must lie on or after it (before_transfer_start). It stays a date when a reopen moves the transfer's first period into the reopened one, so that period's own earlier payday is not planned. Created with no period named and no first date after the period has started, it counts from the day it was created (D-493). The primary occurrence of a period counts when its salary came on or after that day, or when it is the salary the transfer was made from (by key; amended by D-520). Amended by D-610: the first counted day is the start of the period (or the day it was made, D-493); a main-income transfer counts from its first counted period (starts_seq), by number.
decisions.why: The handover's trap: a transfer created in a merged period had its first period moved into the reopened one, which then had its own occurrence of a payday the transfer never knew (the root of M2).
rejected: Freezing first_seq through a reopen: the registry merges validity for every record kind alike.

decisions.title: Due dates of occurrences
decisions.decision: A fixed-day occurrence is due on its date, never capped. A pay-date occurrence is due on the actual pay date plus the offset (0 to 31 days), never after the last day of the period that contains the actual pay date; for the primary income the actual pay date is the period's start, whatever moved it. Answers Q-224: a fixed-day transfer has no occurrence in a period that does not contain its date. Amended by D-610 and D-611: a main-income occurrence is due on its period's start plus the offset; a fixed day's due date is its date moved by its weekend rule.
decisions.why: What the bank does: a standing order runs on its calendar date whatever the salary does.

decisions.title: The transfers' watermark is a date and moves back on every change of the plan
decisions.decision: Each transfer has a watermark by due date (settled_through: every occurrence due up to it is settled), the due date of its next automatic linked occurrence waiting (next_due) and a flag that its plan changed (needs_check). Triggers move the watermark back and set the flag on every change of what the plan derives from: a period inserted, a boundary moved or a period deleted, an income's terms or validity (for transfers choosing it), the transfer's terms or validity, and every removal of a mark. The catch-up then looks at the transfer again from its watermark (D-424). The writes that change the plan (transfer edits and ends, marks, income edits and removals, a primary switch, member removal, every boundary operation and reopen) run that catch-up before they answer, so their answer shows the result; any other path is settled by the next catch-up (my_budgets.caught_up is false until then). Never created twice: one mark per transfer and key, one transaction per mark; none skipped: the watermark passes a due date only once every occurrence due by then is settled.
decisions.why: M1 and the reviewer's dead ends came from a watermark by period that changes of the plan did not move consistently; triggers cover every path, including those of earlier steps.
rejected: A deferred trigger at commit: a test transaction (pgTAP) never commits, and the write's answer would be stale.

decisions.title: What the catch-up removes and what stays
decisions.decision: After a change of the plan the catch-up removes its own marks (and their transactions) whose occurrence is no longer planned or no longer due, and creates the transactions of the automatic linked occurrences due without a mark. It keeps its own mark of an occurrence still planned whatever the new terms: made manual, unlinked, another amount or category (what was recorded on the due date stays; undo leads out). A moved period start is the exception: the catch-up's own marks whose due date the move changed are made again on the new due date (D-491). Ending a transfer turns the catch-up's marks of occurrences it removes into kept marks (by_catch_up false), so nothing recorded goes. A member's mark never goes with a change of the plan: one whose occurrence is no longer planned is listed in the checklist of the period containing its date, flagged (planned false; is_ended when the transfer is not in force there), until undone or until its occurrence is planned again (the salary recorded again). Amended by D-563: the catch-up's own transaction, untouched, follows its occurrence's due date whatever moved it; one made manual or unlinked since stays.
decisions.why: The brief's reconcile step, read together with its rule that an occurrence keeps its mark or transaction when the transfer is made manual, corrected or ended: only an occurrence that is gone or not yet due loses the catch-up's transaction.
rejected: Removing the catch-up's transaction when the transfer is made manual from the current period: the bank did the transfer on its due date.
Removing a member's mark whose occurrence is gone: it would go silently.

decisions.title: The previews run the write and roll it back
decisions.decision: preview_create_transfer, preview_update_transfer and preview_reopen run the write itself in a subtransaction they roll back, and compare the transfers' marks before and after: the catch-up's transactions created and removed, the members' marks whose occurrence is no longer planned or planned again. The create and edit previews give these as counts on every row (created_at_once_count, transactions_removed_count, marks_unplanned_count) and, when the terms govern no occurrence, one row with only the counts (occurrence_date null); preview_reopen gives one row per occurrence (transaction_removed, transaction_created, mark_unplanned, mark_planned_again). preview_end_transfer counts the occurrences it removes and the marks and transactions it keeps. A preview that runs the write takes the budget lock like the write.
decisions.why: Every preview of a change that the catch-up follows must say truthfully what it does; the write's own code is the only way to be sure.

decisions.title: How a preview runs the write
decisions.decision: A preview that runs the write (D-428: preview_create_transfer, preview_update_transfer, preview_reopen, preview_update_income, preview_set_primary_income, preview_move_period_start) takes the budget lock before it reads the revisions and marks it compares, so behind a member's write in flight it waits and then previews what that write left instead of answering record_changed; inside its subtransaction the catch-up step starts afresh (its bound of transactions and its time, D-427), as the write's own statement would. preview_update_transfer with an amount alone (no other term, no p_from_period_id) runs no write and takes no lock: it applies the write's checks of the new terms and answers the plan as it is at the new amount, every count 0.

decisions.title: A period is never without a key; occurrences are found by their key
decisions.decision: Every period has a scheduled pay date as its key (periods.pay_key), derived from the previous period's key (amended by D-561; it was the previous period's projected end plus one, or the next date no period had): keys strictly increase, so several salaries in one month give as many keys, and a reopen and the salary recorded again give the same key. Because a key can then lie a month or more from its period, every lookup of an occurrence goes by the stored key: the periods that can plan a key are the one whose pay_key it is and the one containing the date, wherever they lie (private.transfer_plan_keys). This covers transfer_planned, the checklist's marks planned elsewhere, the catch-up's check of its own marks, the previews' snapshot of marks, deleting a transaction (not done, not deleted) and end_transfer (a mark still planned is not frozen). When both periods give a transfer the same key, it belongs to the earlier one when both are paydays, and is two occurrences when one is a fixed day (amended by D-521, superseded by D-560: an occurrence is told apart by its kind). Answers Q-260. Amended by D-610: periods carry no key any more; an occurrence is found by its period's number or by its date.
decisions.why: With the earlier rule a real payday lost its pay-date transfer after a salary that came 15 or more days early (one transfer for three salaries recorded in one month), and lookups that searched only the neighbouring periods missed keys two periods away: a mark listed twice, deleting its transaction deleted the mark so the catch-up created the transaction again, and ending a transfer froze a mark still planned.
rejected: Keying such a period by its actual start: a key is then not stable across a reopen and the salary recorded on another day.
Searching more neighbouring periods: any fixed window can be exceeded by repeated early salaries.
source: owner-request: coordinator decisions on the independent review of the step 7 redesign (2264e82), M1 with C1, 2026-11-16

decisions.title: The preview asks the parts in order, one at a time (revises D-473)
decisions.decision: useImportPreview asks preview_import_part for part n once part n - 1 has answered, under the batch the import will use, never two at once; an answer is current while its part's rows are the ones now chosen and it was asked after the current answer of the part before. A choice changed in part k asks k to the last again (debounced 400 ms); answers for earlier choices stay on screen marked as being checked. The answer's `parts` must cover the parts asked: a part the database no longer holds (a day old, or pushed out of the 100 a budget keeps by another statement's check) is staged again from there, at most three times, then the page says the checks were not kept, with "Check again". A statement timeout or a lost answer is asked again three times, one, two and three seconds apart, then said with "Check again"; catching_up catches the budget up and asks again. Nothing is asked once the import has started (the run's answers are the truth). The run keeps D-473's busy and lost-answer resends. Files above 100 parts of 500 never reach the preview (D-471).
decisions.why: D-455 and Q-270/Q-274: the database now previews a statement as its write will do it, which only holds if the parts are asked in order; two parts at once would each miss what the other absorbs.
rejected: Keep two previews at once: the second part would not take the first one's absorptions into account.

decisions.title: A resumed import previews only the parts it did not record

The preview starts at the first part not recorded; their rows are shown as recorded and locked (R-IMPORT-362). The totals cover the parts the answer lists: when the check made before the interruption is still kept (a day), they include the recorded parts as checked then, and say so; otherwise they are those of the parts still to send, and say which.
decisions.why: The database knows the written chunks for absorption but does not answer a written part with its record in the preview (Q-290).

decisions.title: The first counted day is compared with the payday, not with the key (amends D-421 and D-493)
decisions.decision: A pay-date transfer's primary occurrence is planned when the salary that started the period came on or after the transfer's first counted day (periods.start_date >= transfers.starts_on), or when the period's key is the key of the salary the transfer was made from (transfers.starts_key: the key of the period it was made from, named or on that period's first day; null when it was made from a later day). The key is an identifier and is never compared with a date. starts_on itself is unchanged (D-421). The test helpers' model derives both from its own memory, and compares the start, not the key.
decisions.why: Since D-490 a key can lie a month or more after its period's start, so comparing it with a date let through what D-493 and D-421 meant to stop: a transaction dated 20 Nov for a transfer made on 22 Nov after an early salary, one dated 5 Jan for a transfer made on 20 Jan after a change of pay day, and a reopen planning the reopened period's own earlier payday (re-check 3, must-fix 1, A to C). Comparing the start alone would drop the salary the transfer was made from once it is recorded on an earlier day (a reopen and the salary again, a moved start), hence the remembered key.
rejected: least(start, key) >= starts_on (the reviewer's suggestion): it also drops a salary that came late, after the transfer was made, when its key lies before the day the transfer was made from, and like the start alone it drops the salary the transfer was made from once recorded earlier.
Moving starts_on with a moved start: a reopen and the salary recorded again on an earlier day are not a moved start, and the key already identifies that salary.

decisions.title: One key, two periods: the same payday or two transfers (amends D-420 and D-490)
decisions.decision: A key two periods give a transfer belongs to the earlier period only when both are paydays: a chosen income's pay date in one and the primary's scheduled pay date in the other (switching between the two). When one of them is a fixed-day date and the other a period's scheduled pay date (a pay-date transfer changed to a fixed day, or back, where a key lies outside its period), they are two transfers: both are planned, and the later period's occurrence is told apart by transfer_occurrences.key_shared (true for its mark only). The API is unchanged: a checklist row and the mark calls name the period and the key, which together are unique; the plan carries key_shared, and every lookup of a mark by its key matches it too. Two marks of one key that are both no longer planned and listed in one period are undone one at a time (the earlier period's first).
decisions.why: With the earlier rule, a transfer changed on 6 Mar to a fixed day 5 from 5 Mar lost its 5 Mar occurrence and transaction, because 5 Mar was also the scheduled pay date of the period 8 Feb.. (re-check 3, must-fix 1, D). One mark per transfer and key cannot hold both, so the later one needs to be told apart.
rejected: Giving the later occurrence another key: no date is guaranteed free, and every lookup of a period by its key would need to undo it.
Re-keying the earlier period's occurrence: its mark and transaction were already recorded under that key.
Separate key spaces for pay-date and fixed-day occurrences everywhere: an edit from a payday to a fixed day on the same date would then lose its mark (R-ACCOUNT-305).

decisions.title: The money flow page, from income to spending (supersedes D-503)
decisions.decision: The Money flow page draws get_money_flow in an SVG of its own (no chart library, a lazy chunk), planned or actual (`?basis=actual`, planned by default, beside `?period=`; each is a history entry, so Back returns to the other): four tiles that are the total row; tiers of incomes, accounts by their chain of transfers, the pool (what stays on the spendable accounts, what is set aside) and the destinations (each category group's planned amount or what it spent, then "not planned" or "left"); bars and bands on one scale (a band too thin to see is drawn at a small minimum thickness, said in the legend), a band that skips a tier keeps a lane there. Left to right whenever every column holds its labels whole beside their bars (from about 600 px of diagram for five tiers); a longer chain up to half again as wide as the card is drawn left to right in its own focusable, named frame that says it scrolls; otherwise top to bottom (no sideways page scroll at 320 px). The thresholds are the developer's to tune by looking. The page may be wider than the usual page (the tables keep the usual width). Labels are HTML, carry their word ("stays … , spendable", "set aside", "planned", "spent … of …") and never cut a figure; a name may be shortened, never two to the same text, whole in its title and the tables. A pattern that means something is wrong (the red hatch) is drawn only where a node's own figure from the read is negative or short, and always with a sentence beside it; the legend names exactly what is drawn in the current layout and basis. Money sent back to an earlier account is drawn left to right as a dashed band with an arrow in its source's colour, named in the legend; top to bottom it is said in a "Sent back" list under the diagram. At most eight incomes, accounts and destinations are drawn: the accounts the drawn incomes arrive on first, then the largest by flow; the others are counted ("and n more: every figure is in the tables"), never summed; an income whose account cannot be drawn says so. A group whose plan is carried by transfers (amount 0) is not drawn as spending (it is in "set aside"); one with its own spending and a transfer share is drawn at its own amount, its label naming the share shown as transfers. A shortfall extends the spendable bar, hatched, by the negative "not planned" or "left", and is said in words. Four tables (incomes, transfers with a link to their transactions, accounts with in, out and what stays, spendable or set aside, and the spending by group, planned and spent) carry every figure with the database's totals and become row blocks below 640 px.
decisions.why: The read now ends at spending (D-524) and the review found the old diagram clipped on a phone, coloured by name and without a legend (S-5, S-6). The owner asked for the money flow diagram by name and to keep it beautiful. Amended after the second screens review: labels were boxed over bands and cut figures, a red hatch appeared without words, the account a salary arrives on could be left out, and Back left the page.
rejected: An "others" bar summing what is not drawn: the page would add figures, and the read gives no aggregate row (D-524).
A sideways scroll frame on a phone (D-503): the flow runs top to bottom instead.
A "left" per account: left is one pooled figure (D-524).
Label boxes on the card colour over the bands, and a lane drawn as a slab under a tier's labels: read as the account named on top of them.
Hatching the set-aside bar whenever more enters it than its figure: nothing is short then.

decisions.title: An occurrence is told apart by the kind of date that produced its key (supersedes D-521 and D-528)
decisions.decision: An occurrence of a planned transfer is identified by its transfer, its key and its kind (transfer_occurrences.kind), a property of the occurrence itself: 'payday' (the salary that started a period, keyed by the period's scheduled pay date), 'income_payday' (a chosen income's pay date in a period where it is not the primary, keyed by that date) or 'fixed_day' (a fixed-day date). A mark stores the kind of the occurrence it was made for, so no other occurrence appearing or going away changes which mark is whose. Keys of one kind are unique to a transfer (period keys are unique, a date lies in one period). Two periods give a transfer the same payday only as one income's salary that started a period ('payday', keyed d) and that same income's own pay date d in another period ('income_payday': the income became or stopped being the primary): that is one occurrence, listed by the earlier period, when the salary came late (its key lies before its period's start: that scheduled pay date came late), or early by less than the projection's 15 days; a salary 15 days or more before its key is another salary, an extra one in a month (two paydays, two occurrences). Two different incomes paid the same day are two paydays (a transfer moved from one to the other can run on each; it was one occurrence before, D-420); and in the period a switch is made in, the old primary's own pay date equal to that period's key is left out only under the same 15 days. A payday and a fixed day with one key are always two occurrences. An edit that changes the kind of an occurrence on the same date in the same period (a payday made a fixed day on that date, a chosen income's pay date made the period's own payday, or back) carries its mark, and so its transaction, over to the new kind, when the old occurrence is planned nowhere else and the new one has no mark of its own (R-ACCOUNT-305 kept). Checklist rows carry occurrence_kind, and mark_transfer_done, skip_transfer, mark_transfer_not_done and undo_transfer_mark take an optional p_occurrence_kind: a period lists at most one row per key and kind, so key and kind name every row, two marks no longer planned with one key included; occurrence_required answers only when a period lists several rows of the transfer and the call names fewer. Amended by D-610: the kinds are 'period', 'income_payday' and 'fixed_day'; occurrences of two kinds are never compared, and there is no same-payday rule.
decisions.why: key_shared was worked out from the plan each time it was read but stored on a mark as a fact: when the earlier of two occurrences with one key went away, or appeared later, the other one took the wrong mark. A correction from the period 5 Feb removed the 5 Mar transaction and listed the 5 Feb one as the 5 Mar occurrence, a reopen did the same, the other way round two transactions were dated 5 Mar and none 5 Feb, and by hand two marks were left that no call could undo (re-check 4, must-fix 1).
rejected: The later of two occurrences with one key (key_shared): not a property of the occurrence, it changes when the other one comes or goes.
The period an occurrence belongs to: a reopen deletes periods, and a moved start or a salary recorded on another day moves the period containing a date.

Two kinds only (payday and fixed day): after an early salary a period's key can equal a later pay date of the same income once it is no longer the primary (the D-528 case), and two real paydays would share one identity.
Separate kinds without carrying a mark over on an edit: an edit from payday to a fixed day on the same date in the same period would lose its mark (R-ACCOUNT-305).

Merging the pay dates of two different incomes that share a date (D-420 as first written): the household counts each income's paydays (D-562), so a pay date of the income a transfer names would be dropped for another income's salary.

decisions.title: A period's key is derived from the previous period's key (answers Q-311; amends D-490)
decisions.decision: Every period's key (periods.pay_key) is the scheduled pay date of the salary that started it, derived when the period is created from the previous period's key, never from its start. While the primary income and its pay dates stay the same (the previous key is a pay date of the terms in force for the new period), it is the next scheduled pay date after the previous key. When they changed (a new pay day, another income made the primary), it is the first pay date of the new terms after the previous key that is no more than the projection's 15 days before the new period's start and, after a primary switch, after the switch day (D-562). The first period's key is its start. Keys strictly increase with the periods, so they are unique without a search for a free date and none is shifted (periods.pay_key_shifted is dropped). A salary early or late, a moved start, a reopen and the salary recorded again on another day never change a key. Nothing is deployed (D-450), so every existing key may have changed once.
decisions.why: The owner's decision on Q-311 (option 1): keys stay the same when a start moved later and the next period is reopened and its salary recorded again (scen7c I2: the mark made by hand stays planned, the December transfer is not to do again), and after a change of pay day the keys return to their own periods instead of naming the next payday for good, the standing condition behind must-fix 1.
rejected: Deriving from the previous period's start (D-490 as first written): a moved start or a salary recorded again on another day changes the key, and after a change of pay day every key names the next payday for good.
The next pay date after the previous key also at a change of pay day: a change from the 25th to the 26th would key the December salary 26 Nov, a month early for good.
Remembering the keys of a reopened period's successors (Q-311 option 2): more state for the same result.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for database fix round 4 (re-check 4), decision on Q-311 (option 1), 2026-11-17
code: supabase/migrations/20261120100000_money_flow.sql

decisions.title: A pay-date transfer happens once per pay date of its income, whatever the primary does (amends D-527)
decisions.decision: The owner's rule: a transfer on payday of an income happens once for every pay date of that income from the transfer's first date on, whichever income is the primary and however often the primary changes; never zero times and never twice. How the occurrence is keyed and which period lists it is an implementation matter. A switch still counts for the transfers from the period after the one it is made in and never rewrites what is already recorded or marked (D-527 kept for that). Pay dates of either income after the switch day are all planned: in the switch period a transfer naming the old primary keeps that period's own payday and also has the old primary's pay dates after the switch day, as a non-primary income's are; the new primary's first period after the switch is keyed by its first pay date after the switch day (D-561), so a pay date the switch period planned as the new primary's own is never taken for it. private.primary_incomes keeps the switch day (switched_on). A transfer naming no income follows the primary: one occurrence per period. transfer_overview.next_due_date and what the catch-up then records come from the same plan (R-ACCOUNT-464). preview_set_primary_income runs the switch and answers what is true, something due at once included.
decisions.why: Re-check 4, must-fix 2: after a switch on 12 Dec from Ann (paid on the 25th) to Ben (the 10th), Ann's 25 Dec and Ben's 10 Jan were never recorded although both were paid, and next_due_date said 10 Jan.
rejected: Counting the switch from its own period: the current period's occurrences, already due and recorded, would be re-planned (D-527).
Leaving the old primary's later pay dates to the next period: the stretched switch period contains them, and the next period starts after them.

decisions.title: What the app recorded by itself sits on its occurrence's due date (amends D-424 and D-491)
decisions.decision: A transaction the catch-up made for an automatic linked occurrence, which nobody touched since, is dated on that occurrence's due date, always. When the due date moves for any reason (a moved start, a salary early or late that moved a period's end and so capped an offset, another offset, the same payday now listed by another period, a kind carried over by an edit), the catch-up's own mark goes with its transaction and is made again on the new due date at the terms in force there (once due, when that date is still ahead). Left exactly as the member left it: a mark of their own, an occurrence made manual or unlinked from its category since (should-fix 5), a transaction a member edited (its revision moved). One rule, in the catch-up; move_period_start relies on it. D-424's 'keeps its own mark of an occurrence still planned whatever the new terms' now holds for everything but the date.
decisions.why: The owner's requirement in re-check 4: an untouched app transaction is always on its occurrence's due date; the reviewer noted an offset transaction left on its old date after an early salary shortened its period, and a start moved after the transfer was unlinked removed the transaction and did not make it again.
rejected: Re-dating in place: the amount and category would then not be the terms in force on the new date, unlike a reopen and the salary recorded again (as D-491).
Re-dating only at a moved start (D-491 as worded): every other change of a due date left transactions off their dates.

decisions.title: The guard of an income deleted outright belongs to its period (amends D-492)

decisions.title: Only a transfer into a set-aside account leaves the spendable pool (amends D-524)

A linked transfer into an everyday account (current, cash, credit_card, other: a cash wallet) never leaves the spendable pool: its share is planned spending and its transactions are spent, like any other. The three balances stay exact: income = set aside + spendable = set aside + planned + not planned = set aside + spent + left; planned and spent then agree with period_summaries.

decisions.title: How the money flow places its labels and routes its bands
decisions.decision: Left to right, each label sits in the gap right of its bar, centred on it, as plain text with a halo in the card's colour over the pale bands; every bar keeps the room its label needs on the cross axis, and bars and lanes move a few rounds towards what they are joined to (the accounts' tiers may change order) so bands run level with their ends. Top to bottom, each tier is a row of bars (a band that skips the tier is a pale part of the row), then its labels on the plain card in the bars' order, each in the column under its bar while that is free, then the bands to the next tier starting with a thin echo of the bars. The headings name incomes, accounts (once, over all their tiers), the pool and the destinations; the middle tiers have no title of their own. Neighbouring bands are separated by a hairline in the card's colour. A band has the colour of where it comes from; a band into a category group has the group's colour.
decisions.why: The reviewer and the coordinator found that a newcomer read the slab under a tier's labels as the account named on top of it, and the labels were tied to their bars by colour alone; "Then to" said nothing.
rejected: Leader lines from each bar to a stacked list of labels: they cross the labels above them on a phone.
A chart library: D-503 and D-545 keep the drawing app-owned.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the money flow polish round (diagram and test gaps), 2026-11-17

decisions.title: A checklist or preview row says its kind of date only where a twin would read the same
decisions.decision: Rows are told apart by period, key and kind (D-560) everywhere the page keys them. A row says what kind of date it is only when another row of the same transfer in the same list has the same due date (or neither has one, two ticks no longer planned): “on the payday that started the period” (payday), “on its chosen income’s payday” (income_payday), “on its fixed day” (fixed_day), in French « au jour de paie qui a ouvert la période », « au jour de paie de son revenu choisi », « à son jour fixe »; the same words complete the names of that row’s buttons (“Skip “Savings, on its fixed day” this time”). Ordinary rows say nothing more, and the key is never shown.
decisions.why: Two rows of one transfer with one key in one period exist (D-560) and otherwise read exactly the same, buttons included; saying the kind on every row would be noise for the usual household.
rejected: Saying the kind on every row: noise on the rows that are never confused.
Naming the income (“on Ben’s payday”): the checklist row does not carry the income of its occurrence, and the transfer’s income now may not be the one an older occurrence had.
Showing the key: keys are identifiers, never dates to show (D-490).

decisions.title: The primary switch and the transfer previews say what the database now does
decisions.decision: The make-primary dialog says, when payday transfers are planned: a transfer that names an income keeps happening on each of that income’s paydays, whichever income is the primary; one on “The main income” follows the new primary income from its next payday, which starts the next period; nothing already recorded or ticked changes (D-562). The transfer previews say a removed transaction of the app is removed because its date is no longer planned or its due date moves (D-563), and when the same preview also records transactions at once, that a transaction whose due date moves counts once in each, nothing being lost, and that the preview does not say which ones move (Q-350). The note that a moved transaction counts once in each shows wherever transfer counts show both a removal and a creation, not only for a moved start.
decisions.why: The previous sentence (“In this period nothing about them changes”) became untrue with D-562, and “for a date that is no longer planned” is untrue for a transaction re-dated under D-563. The previews give counts only, so a move cannot be told from a loss and a new transaction.
rejected: Wording every removal and creation pair as a move: the counts can be a removal of one occurrence and a creation of another.

decisions.title: The money flow’s actual table has a Left column; the share words name what is set aside

Planned keeps two columns. A group’s share carried by transfers is said “… set aside by transfers” on both bases (it covers only transfers into set-aside accounts, D-565), and the legend and the table’s help say that a transfer into an everyday account, a cash wallet, counts as spending.

The sum is used only for that comparison and is never shown; each committed figure is shown as the database gives it.

CHF 43.82 for subscriptions" with no warning. A comparison of figures the database gives shows no new figure, so C-LOGIC-003 and "no client arithmetic to show a figure" hold; a flag in the reads would be cleaner and can replace it later.
rejected: Warning only when one committed figure alone exceeds the plan: CHF 30 of subscriptions and CHF 30 of transfers in a CHF 40 plan would read as inside the plan.

decisions.decision: The screen sent no date when the field was empty, and reopen_previous_period then ends the reopened period at its projection (contract: "or at its projection when omitted"); in the walk-through that made the period run to 24.02.2027 with the next pay day 25.02.2027, a month after the salary that had not arrived. The rule is the database's and is left alone; the screen now always names the day (required, filled in with the next pay day the app announces, editable), and its preview says what the period will then run to.
decisions.why: A person who says the salary has not arrived yet expects it soon; an empty field silently meant "next month". Changing what the projection means is a database decision for the owner (Q-365).
rejected: Working around the projection on the client (computing a nearer date from the schedule): pay-date logic lives in the database (C-LOGIC-001, C-LOGIC-003).
Keeping the field optional with a warning: the surprising default would still be one click away.

decisions.title: The review's categories are set with the existing per-row calls, one row after another
decisions.decision: The row picker and the "one category for several" bar use update_transaction then confirm_import per row, sequentially, never in parallel, stopping at the first refusal. The bulk bar offers the leaves in force now; a row dated where the chosen category is not in force is refused by the database and the run stops there and says so.
decisions.why: The household walk-through had 75 rows to categorise through Actions, Edit, Save, Confirm. No call sets a category and confirms in one step, or does so for several rows; inventing one is a database decision (Q-366). Sequential calls keep the count truthful and the stop exact.
rejected: Parallel calls: a failure would leave an unknown set saved and the count would not say which.
Continuing after a refusal: the brief asks to stop at the first failure.

decisions.title: Offline, a save is refused with "nothing was saved"; it never waits to go out later
decisions.decision: Writes no longer pause while the browser is offline (TanStack Query's default for mutations): every write through the app's one mutation hook, and the review's category calls, first checks navigator.onLine and, offline, is refused before anything is sent, with "You are offline: nothing was saved"; the form keeps what was typed. Reads still wait for the connection and resume by themselves, under an app-wide "You are offline" notice. The import's sending loop keeps its own handling of network failures (it retries a part, then stops and says what was recorded, R-IMPORT-369).
decisions.why: In the walk-through a save offline left the button on "Saving…" and the write went out by itself when the connection returned, possibly minutes later and after the household had changed the same record elsewhere; a budget write the user no longer sees happening is more surprising than a clear refusal. navigator.onLine false is reliable (offline for sure); true does not prove a connection, and a failed call then says it could not reach the server, as before.
rejected: Holding the write and saying it will go out once the connection is back: the household may close the tab or change the record meanwhile, and a concurrency refusal would then arrive out of context.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the final fix round after the household walk-through, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: An ended session is told apart from a sign-out by a short-lived mark in local storage
decisions.decision: Signing out writes the time to local storage (shared by the browser's tabs); a session that disappears (any auth event with no session after one, or a stored Supabase session that does not restore at start) more than a minute after the last sign-out is reported as ended on the sign-in page. Typed values are not kept: keeping them would mean storing a form's content in the browser across users and budgets, which is neither trivial nor safe.
decisions.why: The walk-through's session died mid-form and the user landed on sign-in with no word. Supabase reports an expired and a requested sign-out with the same event.
rejected: Keeping what was typed in session storage and restoring it after sign-in: another user may sign in on the same tab, and a restored form may belong to a budget the user no longer has.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the final fix round after the household walk-through, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: The hosted migrations are checked by hand before a deploy, not by the Deploy workflow
decisions.decision: docs/deployment.md makes "npx supabase migration list --remote" and "npx supabase db push --remote --dry-run" a numbered manual step before every deployment (and before the first one), because the Deploy workflow builds and uploads the app without knowing whether the hosted database has the release's migrations. No database credential or access token is added to CI. Backups are the owner's own data-only dumps (auth, public and private schemas, without the migration-filled private.period_keyed_tables), restored onto a project whose migrations were pushed first, as rehearsed on the local stack.
decisions.why: The final review found the guide silent on backups and on the migration check. A CI check would need the database password or a Supabase access token as a repository secret, which the owner has not asked for; the free plan's own backups could not be verified from the repository or the CLI.
rejected: A CI job that pushes or checks migrations: it needs secrets in CI (brief: none).
A full dump of every schema: the restore is refused on the storage tables and collides on the migration-filled registry table (seen locally).

decisions.title: Three kinds of schedule, each with an identity nothing else can disturb (supersedes D-520, D-527, D-561, D-562 and D-566; amends D-420, D-421, D-422, D-430, D-490 and D-560)
decisions.decision: The owner's decision after five fix rounds: a pay-date transfer is no longer matched against the salary that started a period. Three kinds, never merged, replaced or compared: (1) 'On the main income's payday' (a transfer naming no income, or one whose income is not in force there or was deleted): one occurrence for every period from the transfer's first counted period on, due on the period's start (the day its salary came, whatever started it) plus the offset, never after its last day; identified by the period's number (transfer_occurrences.occurrence_seq), which a reopen and the salary recorded again, a moved start, an early or late salary and a primary switch leave as it is. (2) 'On <income>'s payday' (a transfer naming an income in force in the period): one occurrence for every scheduled pay date of that income (its pay day and weekend rule in force in the period containing the date), due that day plus the offset, never after the period's last day, whether or not that income is the primary and whenever its salary is recorded; identified by that date. An income that ends, is added later or is deleted bounds the dates as before (D-492, D-564). (3) 'On a fixed day': one occurrence per calendar date, identified by the scheduled date, due on it moved by the weekend rule (D-611). Periods carry no key any more (periods.pay_key, private.primary_incomes and its trigger, the switch day and the same-payday comparison are removed); the budget's primary_since_seq stays for the reopen's 'made_primary' row. A transfer counts from starts_on (its first counted day, for dates) and starts_seq (its first counted period, for its own occurrence: the period it was made in, or the next one when made after that period's first day with no period named). A period stretched by a switch (25 Nov to 9 Jan) has one occurrence of a main-income transfer and, for one naming Ann (25th), her 25 Nov and 25 Dec. A household that wants a transfer to follow the day the main salary really arrives names no income; one that wants it to follow a particular income's calendar names that income.
decisions.why: Every defect of re-checks 1 to 5 came from treating an income's pay date and a period's start as possibly the same payday: keys derived from history drift out of their periods (a month ahead after two salaries in a month, behind after a long period), a 15-day comparison then fails, and one remembered switch day per period drops dates when there are two (re-check 5, M1 and M2). With identities that nothing else can move, the defects cannot exist.
rejected: Patching the derivation of keys again (a sixth round): each patch moved the boundary where a payday is doubled or dropped.
Identifying a main-income occurrence by the period's start: a moved start or the salary recorded again on another day would change it.
Keeping 'naming the primary is naming none' (R-ACCOUNT-310): it needs the primary's history per period and brings back the same-payday comparison.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for database fix round 5 (re-check 5, the three kinds of schedule), 2026-11-17

decisions.title: A fixed-day transfer has a weekend rule (answers Q-261)
decisions.decision: A fixed-day transfer takes a weekend rule, the same choices an income has ('none', 'previous', 'next', 'nearest'; default 'none'): transfer_versions.weekend_rule, create_transfer / update_transfer / the previews' p_weekend_rule, transfer_overview.weekend_rule and get_transfer_terms.weekend_rule. The occurrence stays its scheduled date (occurrence_date, listed by the period containing it); its due date is that date moved off a Saturday or Sunday by the rule (it may then lie a day or two outside that period). A pay-date transfer takes none (invalid_schedule).
decisions.why: A bank runs a standing order due on a weekend on a working day; the due date, the overdue flag and the catch-up's transaction date should match it (Q-261). Keeping the identity on the scheduled date means changing the rule moves no mark.
rejected: Identifying the occurrence by its moved date: changing the rule would strand its mark.
Listing it by the period containing its due date: a version change at a period boundary could drop a date.

decisions.title: next_due_date is the first occurrence due today or later with no mark (amends R-ACCOUNT-464)

Moving the clock to that day produces exactly that occurrence, except for a fixed day whose weekend rule puts its due date before the start of a period that does not exist yet (its transaction or its to-do row comes once the period exists, the day it starts, dated its due date); the walk checks it that way.

rejected: Comparing next_due_date with the plan function itself: it would agree with any defect the plan has.

decisions.title: A preview says how many transactions move (answers Q-350)
decisions.decision: Every preview with transfer counts also answers how many of the catch-up's transactions it removes and makes again for the same occurrence (its due date moved): transactions_moved_count on the create and edit preview rows, transfer_transactions_moved on preview_update_income, preview_set_primary_income, preview_move_period_start and the two pay-date previews, and a 'transaction_moved' row in preview_reopen. A moved transaction still counts once removed and once created (the counts keep their meaning); moved says how many of those are one occurrence re-dated. It is exact because an occurrence's identity never changes (D-610).
decisions.why: Q-350: the screens could not tell a move from a loss and a new transaction.
rejected: Leaving Q-350 open: the identity is now stable, so the count is cheap and truthful.
Taking moves out of the removed and created counts: the screens already read those.

decisions.title: The carry-over of a mark on a change of kind does not depend on the call's arguments
decisions.decision: update_transfer looks at the occurrences its terms govern before and after the edit whatever arguments it carries (a new income alone changes the kind too; re-check 5, S1). A mark (and its transaction) goes over to the new occurrence when, in the same period, the old occurrence's day (a period's own: the day its salary came; a chosen income's pay date; a fixed day's scheduled date) equals the new one's, exactly one old and one new occurrence meet there, the old one is planned nowhere now and the new one has no mark of its own. It is a one-time conversion at the edit; the plan never compares kinds.
decisions.why: R-ACCOUNT-305 stays; re-check 5 showed it needed p_schedule in the call, and the reviewer's leftover case (c2) showed a second mark on the new occurrence could collide.
rejected: Carrying a mark over by date alone across periods: two periods could hand the same mark to two occurrences.

decisions.title: The previews and end_transfer see every mark: bounded by period number, not by days
decisions.decision: The marks a write can change are found by the period that lists their occurrence (a period's own by its number, a dated one by the period containing its date), from the earliest period the write can change (the period before a moved boundary, the reopened one, the edit's first period): transfer_marks_snapshot takes a period number. end_transfer looks at all of the transfer's catch-up marks. The windows of 93 days before a period are gone: with keys gone no identity lies outside its period, however long the period or old the mark.
decisions.why: Re-check 5: a key three months behind fell outside the 93-day window; a long period could too.

decisions.title: Every checklist and preview row says what its occurrence is for (supersedes D-600)
decisions.decision: With three kinds whose identities are a period's number or a date (D-610, D-617), every row says what it is for, not only twins: “for the period 23.10.2026 to 24.11.2026” (a period's own, its number looked up among the periods the page has), “on the payday of “Ben”, 10.12.2026” (income_name and the scheduled date), “fixed day 01.12.2026, moved off the weekend” (when the due date differs from the scheduled date); in French « pour la période du … au … », « au jour de paie de « Ben », le … », « jour fixe du …, déplacé hors du week-end ». A mark kept with another period's number is listed by the latest period only when its own period no longer exists (a reopen), so it says “kept from the period a reopen merged into this one, not this period’s own”. The buttons of a transfer listed more than once complete its name with the same words. A preview row of a named income's payday names the income the form chose (preview rows carry no income name).
decisions.why: A 'period' row has no date to show, and two rows of one transfer can share a due date (two pay dates capped at the period's end) or be of two kinds on one date: saying the kind only for twins (D-600) no longer tells them apart, and the period's number is not a thing to show.
rejected: Showing the period's number: an identifier, not something a household reads.
Saying the kind only where twins read the same (D-600): the kind words no longer name a row once two rows of one kind share a due date.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the screens round after database round 5, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: The make-primary dialog and the transfer previews say what round 5 does (supersedes D-601)
decisions.decision: The make-primary dialog says that only the periods' boundaries change and nothing about the transfers is checked again; a transfer on a named income keeps that income's own paydays whichever is the main income; one on the main income's payday stays once per period and follows the new main income only through the periods' starts. It no longer says that nothing recorded changes (the moved end can move what the app recorded; the counts say so). The previews now count moves (D-614), so a move is said as a move (D-654) instead of a possibility.
decisions.why: D-610 and the round-5 database: a switch changes only the boundaries (contract item 11); the old note's “follows the new primary income from its next payday” and “Nothing already recorded or ticked changes” were no longer exact.
rejected: Keeping the D-601 wording: it describes the round-4 matching that D-610 removed.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the screens round after database round 5, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: The transfer form's choice is the occurrence kind
decisions.decision: The form holds the kind ('period', 'income_payday', 'fixed_day') rather than the schedule: the schedule sent is 'day_of_month' for a fixed day and 'pay_date' otherwise; a named income's payday needs its income (validation.incomeRequired) and the income list no longer offers “The main income”; the offset is offered for both paydays; the weekend rule (default none) only for a fixed day, sent with it on create and with any edit of a fixed day's schedule. An edit to the main income's payday clears the income. The values typed for another kind are kept while the member switches, and sent only for the kind chosen.
decisions.why: Three plain options a household understands map one to one onto what the database plans; “The main income” as an item in a list of incomes hid that it is another kind of schedule (once per period).
rejected: A two-way choice (after payday or fixed day) with the main income as the first income: it reads as if the main income were just another income.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the screens round after database round 5, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: A moved transaction is said once, as a move
decisions.decision: Where a preview counts removed, created and moved transfer transactions (the create and edit previews, a moved start, an income's new terms or a new main income, an early or expected salary): when removed and created both equal moved, only “It moves N transactions … to their new due dates” is said; otherwise the removed and created sentences are said and then “Of these, N are transactions moved to their new due dates: each counts once as removed and once as recorded.” The page compares the counts only; it never subtracts moved from removed.
decisions.why: “1 removed, 1 created, 1 moved” reads as three things; subtracting would put a figure on the page that the database did not answer (C-LOGIC-003).
rejected: Showing removed minus moved: a figure worked out by the page.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the screens round after database round 5, 2026-11-17

decisions.title: The money flow's reconciling line: one quiet sentence per side that differs
decisions.decision: Under the four tiles, in small muted text with a scale icon, one sentence per difference that is not zero: “The other pages show incomes of CHF 10’250.00: this page’s CHF 10’000.00 plus CHF 250.00 of extra income, which is not part of the plan.” (both bases, when extra_income_left_out is not 0); “The other pages show CHF 5’488.00 planned: this page’s CHF 3’900.00 plus CHF 1’588.00 that transfers put aside.” (planned basis, set_aside_transfers_planned); “The other pages show CHF 3’905.50 spent: this page’s CHF 2’905.50 plus CHF 1’000.00 that transfers put aside.” (actual basis, set_aside_transfers_spent). The figures are the total row's summary columns, this page's tile figure (incomes, planned spending, spent) and the difference column: the database guarantees the first is the sum of the other two. “The other pages” rather than one page's name: the dashboard shows the income, the progress, budget and compare pages the planned and spent totals. Nothing is said when all differences are zero.
decisions.why: The flow and the other pages use the words “Incomes”, “Planned” and “Spent” for different figures (D-618); a household comparing them to the rappen needs the reason where the tiles are, without a table of its own.
rejected: Showing the other pages' figures as more tiles: four tiles already; a fifth and sixth figure would read as more money.
Always showing the line: noise when nothing differs (no extra income, no transfer into a set-aside account).
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the screens round after database round 5, 2026-11-17

openQuestions.question: When a period start moves onto or before a debt's opening and back again, how should the debt's interest come back, and should the later entries follow the history?
openQuestions.context: D-386 removes the period's interest entry when its start moves to on or before the opening (a trigger in the step 4 migration, private.drop_interest_before_opening) and adds nothing when it moves later again, because interest is computed once, when the period is created. So after a start moves onto the opening day and back, the debt is lower for good by the removed entry (120.00 in the re-review), and the next period's entry keeps the balance it was computed on (debt_interest.balance 1 212 000 while the history's balance before it is now 1 200 000). Options: (a) refuse the move while the period holds an interest entry of a debt opened on or after the new start (a refusal code, shown by preview_move_period_start as it already counts interest_removed): the history stays exact and nothing is lost, at the cost of a restriction; (b) keep the entry but mark it suspended while the start is on or before the opening, and restore it when the start moves after the opening again: the round trip is exact, but while suspended the later entries' balance disagrees by the suspended amount; (c) on any removal, recompute every later entry of that debt from the history: balance always agrees, but amounts the member has seen change, and a move back still loses the entry unless combined with (b). Recommended: (a). Any option changes the step 4 migration's trigger and its preview, which under D-450 is a new migration (or the money-flow rewrite), so it was not fixed in this round.
source: owner-request: coordinator brief for the step 6 database fix round 2 (re-review at 747686c), 2026-11-16
